MaxIM: Maximally Informative Incremental Summarization via Reinforcement Learning

Jihwan Jeong Affiliation: Google Research    Guy Tennenholtz ††thanks: Work done while at Google. Affiliation: Noetive    Yinlam Chow Affiliation: Google DeepMind{jihwanjeong, yinlamchow, cwhsu, cboutilier}@google.com, guytenn@gmail.com    Chih-Wei Hsu Affiliation: Google Research    Craig Boutilier Affiliation: Google Research
Abstract

AI systems must often maintain bounded memory of unbounded interaction histories. However, optimizing the memory representation, and its updates, for downstream task utility is difficult for standard reinforcement learning (RL) due to severe credit assignment bottlenecks induced by sparse, delayed rewards. We introduce MaxIM (Maximally Informative Incremental Memory), a framework that formulates incremental summarization as a capacity-constrained, information-theoretic reward-shaping problem. Grounded in value suboptimality bounds, we show that bounding sequential information loss motivates maximizing the predictive log-likelihood of future, task-relevant targets, a variational lower bound on predictive sufficiency. We introduce a recursive consistency condition to ensure summaries are grounded by maximizing mutual information (MI) with the observed history. We mitigate credit assignment issues with a parameterized asymmetric critic that computes step-wise variational MI bounds for dense reward shaping. Empirical evaluation on long-horizon scientific reading and multi-turn dialogue benchmarks shows that MaxIM outperforms RL, supervised fine-tuning, and prompt-focused baselines on factual grounding, comprehensive autorater metrics, and downstream task utility across strict token budgets and extended horizons, without the need for expensive human preference labels.

1 Introduction

A critical challenge facing AI agents in continuous, streaming environments—from real-time personalization [1, 2] to long-horizon dialogue [3, 4]—is the inability to retain unbounded context. Despite the expanded context windows of modern large language models (LLMs), processing ever-growing interaction logs frequently degrades reasoning performance due to “lost in the middle” phenomena [5]. While heuristic memory buffers (e.g., MemGPT [6]) and RL-based memory models (e.g., MemAgent [7], Mem-α\alpha [8]) offer practical mechanisms for context management, agents ultimately need rigorous methods to actively compress these streams into a fixed-capacity working memory.

We assume a trainable history/context summarization policy manages this bounded memory state, while a separate, frozen action agent uses it to choose how to act in the environment. In this setting, the objective of a memory system is to maximize downstream task utility, RtaskR_{\text{task}}. In principle, optimizing a summarizer using reinforcement learning (RL) on RtaskR_{\text{task}} yields an optimal compression strategy. However, in long-horizon settings, task rewards are notoriously sparse and delayed, inducing extreme credit assignment failures in RL—the policy receives insufficiently granular feedback to learn which observation-stream features are predictive of task success. Conversely, optimizing for surface-level text reconstruction [9, 10] discards deeper latent intents needed for effective future inference.

To bridge this gap, we develop MaxIM (Maximally Informative Incremental Memory), a novel RL framework that addresses credit assignment with dense information-theoretic reward shaping. Leveraging bounds from state abstraction theory, we show that the performance gap induced by constrained memory is bounded by sequential information loss. We show that bounding this loss motivates maximizing the predictive log-likelihood of future, task-relevant target variables YtY_{t}, a variational lower bound on predictive sufficiency. However, optimizing an LLM purely for future prediction can induce severe hallucinations (i.e., fabricating plausible-sounding text that aligns with the task/target, but is disconnected from actual observations). To prevent this, we derive a recursive consistency regularizer that maximizes the mutual information (MI) with the immediate history, substantially suppressing ungrounded generation.

To optimize this dual-objective, MaxIM employs RL with asymmetric context (see Figure 1). We leverage synthetic datasets to train a parameterized critic using supervised cross-entropy minimization, which computes step-wise baseline-normalized variational predictive likelihood (VPL) bounds [11], thus providing dense shaping rewards to the policy. We update the policy using standard policy gradient methods equipped with a backward-discounted reward-to-go to account for temporal error accumulation, while gradually annealing the shaping weight to ensure that late-stage training directly optimizes downstream task utility.

Our contributions are: (1) We develop MaxIM, a principled RL framework for capacity-constrained generative memory that solves the sparse credit assignment bottleneck via dense information-theoretic reward shaping. (2) We link value suboptimality bounds to sequential information loss across both static and dynamic partially observable environments, deriving two complementary regularizers: predictive sufficiency and recursive consistency. (3) We offer an effective training architecture using scalable synthetic data generation and a unified asymmetric critic to compute calibrated variational lower bounds, obviating the need for human preference labels. (4) We demonstrate MaxIM’s efficacy on diverse benchmarks—a dynamic multi-turn user simulator and a novel arXiv scientific reading task—achieving superior factual grounding, token-budget Pareto efficiency, and task success.

2 Related Work

Incremental Summarization and Memory Buffers.

Traditional summarization processes entire documents to generate static outputs [12, 13], whereas incremental summarization recursively updates a summary as streaming information arrives [14]. While early text streaming systems relied on clustering algorithms [15], modern neural approaches exploit structural representations (e.g., JSON states) for incremental updates [10]. A parallel line of work compresses long contexts in continuous space—including learned soft-prompt or embedding compression [16, 17, 18] and optimal-transport token-merging or KV-cache compression. These methods require either retraining the downstream model to consume continuous latents or white-box access to internal model activations. By contrast, we maintain a discrete, human-readable text memory under a token budget KK, allowing it to interface directly with any frozen black-box agent. Recently, sophisticated memory buffer methods have emerged to manage unbounded LLM contexts. The closest analogs to our setup are memory systems such as MemGPT [6], Mem-α\alpha [8], and MemAgent [7]. While MemGPT and Mem-α\alpha focus on tool-calling, MemAgent learns an explicit, generative memory update policy using RL, as we do. However, these methods rely on sparse task rewards which can exacerbate hallucination and historical drift due to credit assignment failures. MaxIM builds on this foundation by introducing theoretically derived, dense MI regularizers that explicitly guide the retention of task-relevant information.

Preference Modeling and Information-Theoretic Shaping.

Modern alignment techniques like RLHF [19, 20] and RLAIF [21, 22] typically train heuristic reward models on pairwise rankings using the Bradley-Terry model [23]. While successful for general alignment, these scalar models lack formal guarantees w.r.t. preserving task-critical information and struggle with long-horizon credit assignment. While MaxIM is similar to RLAIF in its use of an oracle AI for offline data generation, we depart from preference-based rewards. Instead, we frame context compression as a reward shaping problem [24]. Specifically, by training a critic to compute calibrated VPL bounds, MaxIM provides dense, step-by-step information-theoretic rewards. This directly optimizes rigorous MI lower bounds, promoting predictive sufficiency and factual grounding without the theoretical liabilities of standard preference approximations.

RL with Asymmetric Context.

RL with asymmetric context (or privileged information) trains policies using a critic that has access to oracle information unavailable to the actor [25, 26]. Widely used in robotics to train student policies with expert teachers, we adapt it to LLM memory. By treating future text or latent intents as “oracle hindsight context,” we compute dense information-theoretic rewards that shape the LLM’s summary update policy without expensive human labels.

3 Background

3.1 Capacity-Constrained Memory and Sparse Rewards

Incremental Summarization.

We formalize the environment as a sequential interaction stream. An agent (or actor) engages with an environment, generating actions at∈𝒜a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} given a continuous stream of observations ot∈Ωo_{t}\in\Omega. Optimal decision making generally requires conditioning on the current history Ht=(o1,a1,…,at−1,ot)H_{t}=(o_{1},a_{1},\dots,a_{t-1},o_{t}). Maintaining HtH_{t} indefinitely is computationally intractable for LLMs due to their finite context windows, hence, the agent adopts a summarizer policy πθ​(zt∣zt−1,at−1,ot)\pi_{\theta}(z_{t}\mid z_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t}) that incrementally updates a textual summary zt∈⋃k=1K𝒱kz_{t}\in\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{V}^{k}, where 𝒱\mathcal{V} is the LLM vocabulary and KK is a maximum token budget. The agent’s policy conditions its action choice solely on the capacity-constrained working memory ztz_{t} and the current observation oto_{t} to select its next action ata_{t}.11 1 We assume the agent conditions on memory and the latest observation, though it can use the last kk observations if compute and context permit. We assume the agent is fixed/frozen and focus on training the summarizer for optimal performance.

Sparse Rewards and Regularized MDPs.

The standard RL objective for optimizing policies maximizes expected cumulative task reward: J⁡(θ)=𝔼πθ​[∑tγt​Rtask,t]J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}[\sum_{t}\gamma^{t}R_{\text{task},t}]. However, in long-horizon settings, RtaskR_{\text{task}} can be exceptionally sparse (e.g., evaluated only at the end of a multi-turn dialogue or after reading a full document). This sparsity makes RL challenging due to credit assignment failures. While classic reward shaping [24] injects dense signals without altering the optimal policy via potential functions, this is insufficient in our capacity-constrained setting. Instead, we alter the objective to form a regularized Markov decision process (MDP) [27]. By injecting dense, step-wise information-theoretic auxiliary rewards, we explicitly constrain the policy’s exploration manifold, guiding it to find an effective bounded-memory policy rather than the theoretically infeasible unconstrained optimal (which would require unbounded memory).

A Unified POMDP Formulation.

While our sequence compression formulation applies broadly, our framework models the interaction stream as a partially observable MDP (POMDP). This treats summary ztz_{t} as a textual belief state tracking an unobservable latent state st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}. Crucially, this interpretation gracefully accommodates diverse streaming models, such as:
Dynamic Latent States (e.g., User Simulation): In multi-turn interactions, a user’s underlying persona, intent, or mood acts as a dynamic latent state sts_{t} that evolves sequentially. The summary ztz_{t} tracks this intent to guide the agent’s conversational responses.
Static Latent States and Active Perception (e.g., Goal-directed reading): For tasks like reading a scientific paper to answer eventual questions, the environment state (i.e., full document semantics and golden target answers) is static. However, with bounded context, it becomes fundamentally partially observable. Intermediate actions (e.g., reading the next text chunk) are pure sensing actions, while the summary ztz_{t} serves as the belief state, accumulating the necessary sufficient statistics from the observations to resolve the unobserved target variables (questions) at the terminal step. By viewing both settings through this lens, we bridge incremental summarization and classical belief tracking, and thus establish formal value suboptimality bounds (see Section 4).

3.2 Mutual Information and Representation Learning

Estimating Mutual Information.

Mutual information (MI), denoted I⁡(X,Y)I(X;Y) and defined as I⁡(X,Y)=𝔼P⁡(x,y)​[log⁡P⁡(x,y)P⁡(x)​P​(y)]I(X;Y)=\mathbb{E}_{P(x,y)}\!\big[\log\frac{P(x,y)}{P(x)P(y)}\big], measures the reduction in uncertainty about a random variable YY given knowledge of XX. Estimating MI in high-dimensional continuous or discrete spaces is difficult. One prevalent approach in representation learning, contrastive predictive coding (CPC), uses the InfoNCE loss [28]. While successfully applied to learning continuous embeddings, InfoNCE has been proven to be strictly upper-bounded by log⁡N\log N, where NN is the batch size [29]. This bound saturates rapidly when modeling high-entropy distributions like autoregressive text generation, limiting its utility as a metric for unbounded optimization.

Variational Bounds.

To overcome this log⁡N\log N limitation, variational approximations based on ff-divergences are often adopted, such as the NWJ [30] or SMILE [31] estimators. However, these estimators are known to suffer from high variance, numerical instability, and extreme hyperparameter sensitivity, particularly when the true MI is large [32]. Because of this, we focus on the VPL bound [11]. By introducing a parameterized variational distribution qϕ​(Y∣X)q_{\phi}(Y\mid X), we leverage the non-negativity of KL divergence to establish a theoretically sound lower bound:

I⁡(X,Y)≥H⁡(Y)+𝔼P⁡(x,y)​[log⁡qϕ​(y∣x)].I(X;Y)\geq H(Y)+\mathbb{E}_{P(x,y)}[\log q_{\phi}(y\mid x)]. (1)

In standard representation learning, maximizing this log-likelihood maximizes I⁡(X,Y)I(X;Y) when the marginal entropy H⁡(Y)H(Y) is constant. In closed-loop POMDPs, the agent’s actions influence future states, causing H⁡(Yt)H(Y_{t}) to become weakly policy-dependent. However, as we prove in Section 4, our framework circumvents this dependency: maximizing predictive log-likelihood directly bounds conditional entropy H⁡(Yt∣zt)H(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}), which bounds the sequential information loss regardless of the marginal H⁡(Yt)H(Y_{t}). This provides a tractable, theoretically rigorous, low-variance surrogate objective that scales naturally to modern LLMs.

4 Methodology: The MaxIM Framework

We frame capacity-constrained incremental summarization as a task of information-theoretic reward shaping. Our objective is to learn a summarizer update policy πθ\pi_{\theta} that dynamically creates and maintains a working memory ztz_{t}, bounded by a strict token limit KK, to maximize downstream task utility RtaskR_{\text{task}}. Crucially, πθ\pi_{\theta} is solely responsible for memory management; a separate, frozen action agent (e.g., a conversational assistant or a question-answering module) conditions on this memory ztz_{t} to act within the environment. Because RtaskR_{\text{task}} is often sparse and delayed in long-horizon streams (e.g., assessed only at the terminal turn TT), standard RL struggles with credit assignment. Our goal is to derive principled, dense shaping rewards that offer step-by-step auxiliary guidance through the optimization landscape.

4.1 Value Suboptimality and Predictive Sufficiency

Maintaining the full observation history Ht=(Ht−1,at−1,ot)H_{t}=(H_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t}) is computationally intractable in streaming environments, forcing systems to compress HtH_{t} into a bounded summary ztz_{t}. To quantify the impact of this compression on downstream task utility, we frame the sequential interaction as a POMDP, treating ztz_{t} as a capacity-constrained Markovian state abstraction [33, 34]. Let YtY_{t} denote the task-relevant target variable at step tt—e.g., static comprehension answers in goal-directed reading (Yt+1=YtY_{t+1}=Y_{t}), or a user’s evolving latent state sts_{t} in multi-turn dialogue—and let μθ\mu_{\theta} denote the trajectory distribution induced by πθ\pi_{\theta} with the frozen action agent πact​(at∣zt,ot)\pi_{\text{act}}(a_{t}\mid z_{t},o_{t}). As detailed in Appendix A.1, we assume: (A1) Target Mediation, where expected task rewards and next-step state-observation transitions depend on (Ht,at)(H_{t},a_{t}) through (Yt,at)(Y_{t},a_{t}) (covering both static targets and closed-loop settings where ata_{t} alters Yt+1Y_{t+1}); (A2) Memory Causality (zt⟂Yt|Htz_{t}\perp Y_{t}\mid H_{t}), meaning πθ\pi_{\theta} updates ztz_{t} from observed history without privileged access to YtY_{t}; and (A3) Compressed Action Selection (at⟂Yt|Ht,zta_{t}\perp Y_{t}\mid H_{t},z_{t}), meaning the actor selects ata_{t} based on (zt,ot)(z_{t},o_{t}) alone.

Theorem 1 (Value Suboptimality Bound; extending [33, 34]).

Let V∗​(Ht)V^{*}(H_{t}) be the optimal expected return achievable with the full observation history, and V∗​(zt)V^{*}(z_{t}) be the optimal expected return achievable using the capacity-constrained summary ztz_{t}. Under Assumptions (A1)–(A3) with rewards bounded in [−Rmax,Rmax][-R_{\max},R_{\max}], the expected suboptimality gap under the induced trajectory distribution μθ\mu_{\theta} is bounded by the sequential information loss Iμθ​(Yt;Ht∣zt)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t}):

𝔼μθ​[|V∗​(Ht)−V∗​(zt)|]≤2​Rmax(1−γ)2​supkIμθ​(Yk;Hk∣zk).\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\theta}}\big[|V^{*}(H_{t})-V^{*}(z_{t})|\big]\leq\frac{\sqrt{2}R_{\max}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\sqrt{\sup_{k}I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{k};H_{k}\mid z_{k})}. (2)

Theorem 1 (proved alongside an approximate-mediation extension in Appendix A.1) establishes that to minimize the value suboptimality gap, it suffices for the agent to minimize sequential information loss Iμθ​(Yt;Ht∣zt)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t}). This observation directly yields our first shaping objective:

Proposition 1 (Predictive Sufficiency).

To minimize the value suboptimality gap under a token budget |zt|≤K|z_{t}|\leq K, the policy can instead maximize the negative conditional entropy −Hμθ​(Yt∣zt)-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}), which we call predictive sufficiency. Introducing a parameterized variational distribution (critic) qϕ​(Yt∣zt)q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}), under (A2) sequential information loss satisfies Iμθ​(Yt;Ht∣zt)=𝔼μθ​[−log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣zt)]−Hμθ​(Yt∣Ht)−Δpost​(ϕ,θ)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\theta}}[-\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})]-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid H_{t})-\Delta_{\mathrm{post}}(\phi;\theta), where Δpost(ϕ;θ)≔𝔼zt∼μθ[DKL(Pμθ(Yt∣zt)∥qϕ(Yt∣zt))]≥0\Delta_{\mathrm{post}}(\phi;\theta)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{z_{t}\sim\mu_{\theta}}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})\,\|\,q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}))]\geq 0. Thus, maximizing 𝔼μθ​[log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣zt)]\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\theta}}[\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})] maximizes a variational lower bound on predictive sufficiency—minimizing an upper bound on Iμθ​(Yt;Ht∣zt)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t}) up to closed-loop filtering-entropy shifts (zero for static targets; Appendix A.2)—without requiring constant marginal entropy Hμθ​(Yt)H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}).

We prove Proposition 1 in Appendix A.2, where Proposition 4 characterizes how budget KK and critic quality enter Eq. (2): since |zt|≤K|z_{t}|\leq K carries at most K​log⁡|𝒱|+log⁡2K\log|\mathcal{V}|+\log 2 nats, information loss obeys a rate-distortion floor decreasing with KK until ztz_{t} is sufficient for YtY_{t}. Maximizing 𝔼μθ​[log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣zt)]\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\theta}}[\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})] approaches this frontier up to Δpost​(ϕ,θ)\Delta_{\mathrm{post}}(\phi;\theta).

4.2 Factual Grounding and Recursive Consistency

While maximizing predictive sufficiency −Hμθ​(Yt∣zt)-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}) ensures the summary retains task-relevant information, optimizing this objective in isolation can introduce a severe failure mode for LLMs:

Lemma 1 (The Hallucination Failure Mode).

Let πθ\pi_{\theta} be a stochastic policy operating under token budget KK. Because the mapping from a complex history HtH_{t} to a sparse downstream target YtY_{t} is many-to-one, optimizing solely for predictive sufficiency maxθ⁡[−Hμθ​(Yt∣zt)]\max_{\theta}[-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})] under-specifies the summary mapping. The policy can achieve the objective by fabricating plausible but ungrounded text that correlates with YtY_{t}, sampled from its pre-trained prior. This maximizes the ungrounded conditional entropy H⁡(zt∣Ht)H(z_{t}\mid H_{t}) and severs the summary’s dependence on the true history.

As argued in Appendix A.3, this lemma implies that an unconstrained policy can satisfy the predictive sufficiency objective by generating idealized, highly probable text that encodes the target YtY_{t} while suppressing I⁡(zt,Ht)I(z_{t};H_{t}) toward the minimum required by the data processing inequality (DPI). This vulnerability aligns with uncertainty quantification research in LLMs [35, 36] showing that high ungrounded conditional entropy H⁡(zt∣Ht)H(z_{t}\mid H_{t}) is a primary indicator of confabulation.

Proposition 2 (Recursive Consistency (Informal)).

To suppress hallucination and promote factual grounding during streaming updates from local context H~t=(zt−1,at−1,ot)\tilde{H}_{t}=(z_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t}), the policy can regularize updates by maximizing the MI between the new summary and its conditioning context: maxθ⁡Iμθ​(zt,H~t)\max_{\theta}I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t}). We refer to this regularizer as recursive consistency.

We formalize and prove Proposition 2 in Appendix A.4. Since Iμθ​(zt,H~t)=Hμθ​(zt)−Hμθ​(zt∣H~t)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t})=H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t})-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t}), maximizing Iμθ​(zt,H~t)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t}) penalizes ungrounded entropy Hμθ​(zt∣H~t)H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t}), while predictive sufficiency prevents ztz_{t} from collapsing into a trivial constant summary (which would drop −Hμθ​(Yt∣zt)-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}) back to −Hμθ​(Yt)-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t})). Because πθ\pi_{\theta} observes only H~t\tilde{H}_{t}, any task-relevant detail omitted from zt−1z_{t-1} is permanently lost unless re-observed: Proposition 5 and Corollary 1 (Appendix A.4) formalize how per-turn losses accumulate, vanishing when KK suffices to update the task-relevant sufficient statistics from H~t\tilde{H}_{t} and showing why myopic single-step compression fails.

4.3 The MaxIM Objective and Unified Asymmetric Critic Training

We operationalize Propositions 1 and 2 into step-wise RL rewards using the local streaming context H~t=(zt−1,at−1,ot)\tilde{H}_{t}=(z_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t}). Computing exact MI online during RL rollouts is intractable; instead, we generate an offline synthetic dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} with privileged access to YtY_{t} (Appendix B) and pre-train a critic qϕq_{\phi} via teacher forcing.

From Sufficiency and Consistency to Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) Rewards.

To turn both objectives into calibrated step-wise rewards, we cast each as a log-likelihood ratio. For predictive sufficiency (Proposition 1), using log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣zt)\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}) as-is conflates summary quality with target difficulty: easy targets score well even when ztz_{t} is uninformative, whereas hard targets score poorly even for thorough summaries. Subtracting a summary-free baseline log⁡qϕ​(Yt)\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t})—independent of ztz_{t} conditional on (Ht,Yt)(H_{t},Y_{t}), leaving the immediate policy gradient of log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣zt)\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}) unbiased—isolates the information ztz_{t} provides about YtY_{t} in PMI form, log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣zt)qϕ​(Yt)\log\frac{q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})}{q_{\phi}(Y_{t})}. For recursive consistency (Proposition 2), I⁡(zt,H~t)=𝔼⁡[log⁡P⁡(H~t∣zt)P⁡(H~t)]=𝔼⁡[log⁡P⁡(zt∣H~t)P⁡(zt)]I(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t})=\mathbb{E}\!\big[\log\frac{P(\tilde{H}_{t}\mid z_{t})}{P(\tilde{H}_{t})}\big]=\mathbb{E}\!\big[\log\frac{P(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t})}{P(z_{t})}\big]. Scoring consistency via backward reconstruction log⁡qϕ​(H~t∣zt)\log q_{\phi}(\tilde{H}_{t}\mid z_{t}) fails to penalize hallucinated claims appended alongside true statements, since fabricated sentences in ztz_{t} need not lower the likelihood of reconstructing H~t\tilde{H}_{t}. Estimating I⁡(zt,H~t)I(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t}) in the forward direction, log⁡P⁡(zt∣H~t)P⁡(zt)\log\frac{P(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t})}{P(z_{t})}, evaluates each token of ztz_{t}: claims unsupported by H~t\tilde{H}_{t} are no more probable given H~t\tilde{H}_{t} than unconditionally, yielding zero or negative log-ratios.

Because both objectives share this conditional-to-unconditional log-ratio structure, at each step tt we query qϕq_{\phi} with the conditioning input present and replaced by a fixed null placeholder—znullz_{\mathrm{null}} when omitting ztz_{t} (e.g., "(no summary available)") to approximate P⁡(Yt)P(Y_{t}), and H~null\tilde{H}_{\mathrm{null}} when omitting (zt−1,at−1,ot)(z_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t}) to approximate P⁡(zt)P(z_{t}). Routing all four queries via mode-specific system instructions (Appendix E.3) trains a single unified critic qϕq_{\phi} via cross-entropy loss on 𝒟\mathcal{D}:

ℒ(ϕ)=−𝔼𝒟[\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\phi)=-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\Big[ λpred​(log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣zt)+log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣znull))\displaystyle\lambda_{\text{pred}}\big(\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})+\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{\mathrm{null}})\big) (3)
+λcons(logqϕ(zt∣H~t)+logqϕ(zt∣H~null))],\displaystyle+\lambda_{\text{cons}}\big(\log q_{\phi}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t})+\log q_{\phi}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{\mathrm{null}})\big)\Big],

with loss weights λpred,λcons>0\lambda_{\text{pred}},\lambda_{\text{cons}}>0. During RL, the frozen qϕq_{\phi} scores ztz_{t} at turn tt via length-normalized PMI using teacher-forced forward passes only (zero critic generation):

rpred,t\displaystyle r_{\text{pred},t} =1|Yt|​∑i=1|Yt|[log⁡qϕ​(Yt,i∣Yt,<i,zt)−log⁡qϕ​(Yt,i∣Yt,<i,znull)],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|Y_{t}|}\sum_{i=1}^{|Y_{t}|}\Big[\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t,i}\mid Y_{t,<i},z_{t})-\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t,i}\mid Y_{t,<i},z_{\mathrm{null}})\Big], (4)
rcons,t\displaystyle r_{\text{cons},t} =1|zt|​∑i=1|zt|[log⁡qϕ​(zt,i∣zt,<i,H~t)−log⁡qϕ​(zt,i∣zt,<i,H~null)].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|z_{t}|}\sum_{i=1}^{|z_{t}|}\Big[\log q_{\phi}(z_{t,i}\mid z_{t,<i},\tilde{H}_{t})-\log q_{\phi}(z_{t,i}\mid z_{t,<i},\tilde{H}_{\mathrm{null}})\Big]. (5)

Proposition 6 (Appendix A.5) formalizes per-step baseline unbiasedness, multi-step/sigmoid trade-offs, the KL decomposition for rcons,tr_{\text{cons},t}, and critic shift bounds (validated in Appendix F.2).

4.4 Policy Update and Algorithm Overview

During RL, the summarizer policy maps (zt−1,at−1,ot)(z_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t}) to an updated summary ztz_{t}. Because discarding critical information early causes irreversible downstream loss, we propagate future task and shaping signals back to each turn tt using a backward-discounted return-to-go Gt,sG_{t,s} at RL step ss.

We map rpred,tr_{\text{pred},t} and rcons,tr_{\text{cons},t} onto a common bounded scale via centered sigmoids:

r^t=ws​(σ⁡(αs​(rpred,t−bs))−12)+wc​(σ⁡(αc​(rcons,t−bc))−12).\hat{r}_{t}=w_{s}\big(\sigma(\alpha_{s}(r_{\text{pred},t}-b_{s}))-\tfrac{1}{2}\big)+w_{c}\big(\sigma(\alpha_{c}(r_{\text{cons},t}-b_{c}))-\tfrac{1}{2}\big). (6)

Here (ws,wc)(w_{s},w_{c}) weighs sufficiency and consistency, respectively, with wc<wsw_{c}<w_{s} so consistency acts as a grounding regularizer and does not dominate sufficiency; and (αs,bs,αc,bc)(\alpha_{s},b_{s},\alpha_{c},b_{c}) are calibrated offline using summaries sampled from the initial pre-RL base policy (Appendix D.3). Centering at −12-\tfrac{1}{2} assigns baseline-quality summaries zero shaping reward (avoiding positive length bias on variable-horizon episodes). Because r^k\hat{r}_{k} is summed across turns k=t,…,Tk=t,\dots,T whereas RtaskR_{\text{task}} is sparse, we scale r^k\hat{r}_{k} by ηshape=1−γ\eta_{\text{shape}}=1-\gamma so accumulated shaping rewards remain balanced against RtaskR_{\text{task}}. Finally, a cosine schedule λs∈[0,1]\lambda_{s}\in[0,1] over RL update iterations ss holds λs=1\lambda_{s}=1 early to resolve credit assignment and decays λs→0\lambda_{s}\to 0 mid-training so late-stage updates optimize RtaskR_{\text{task}} without residual critic bias:

Gt,s=∑k=tTγk−t​(Rtask,k+ηshape​λs​r^k).G_{t,s}=\sum_{k=t}^{T}\gamma^{k-t}\big(R_{\text{task},k}+\eta_{\text{shape}}\lambda_{s}\,\hat{r}_{k}\big). (7)

We update πθ\pi_{\theta} using KL-regularized PPO [37] with group-based relative advantage estimation [38]: for each initial state, GG rollouts are sampled and Gt,sG_{t,s} is standardized at each turn tt via a leave-one-out baseline across the remaining G−1G-1 active rollouts in the group (Algorithm 1, Appendix C).

5 Experiments

We evaluate MaxIM on two complementary streaming benchmarks instantiating our static and dynamic POMDP formulations (Section 4), addressing three research questions:

  • •

    RQ1: Does MaxIM’s information-theoretic reward shaping improve downstream task utility and token-budget Pareto efficiency over state-of-the-art memory baselines?

  • •

    RQ2: How does MaxIM perform on fine-grained atomic-claim grounding and qualitative axes—Truthfulness, Usefulness, and Consistency—under cross-family LLM judges?

  • •

    RQ3: How do MaxIM’s individual reward components (sufficiency PMI, recursive consistency PMI, and mid-training cosine annealing) contribute to task utility and grounding?

5.1 Experimental Setup

Tasks and Environments.

Task 1: arXiv Scientific Reading. The agent incrementally reads 500-token chunks of a paper (up to 2020 in RL; 2525 at test) under a strict K=500K=500 token budget, plus K∈{100,300,800}K\in\{100,300,800\} to test budget scaling. To minimize pretraining leakage, we curate 2,1962{,}196 recent ar5iv papers [39] across nine domains into disjoint critic/SFT (1,2811{,}281), RL (533533), validation (4444), and post-cutoff test (338338) splits, each with five cross-section synthesis multiple choice questions (MCQs) (Appendix B.1). To penalize guessing with no evidence and to evaluate evidence explicitly retained in zTz_{T}, we use Abstain-MCQ Accuracy: given only zTz_{T}, the frozen actor selects A–D or E (“Insufficient information”), earning +1+1 for correct, 00 for E, and −1/3-1/3 for wrong guesses (00 random expectation). An Early-Section Stress Test (332332 held-out papers) probes retention of technical details (design justifications, ablation trade-offs) appearing only in chunks 33–77 across 1313–2222 subsequent updates.

Task 2: WildChat Multi-Turn User Simulation. The agent tracks a user’s evolving latent state under a K=1,024K=1{,}024 token budget using a 10-key JSON belief schema (goals, preferences, constraints, affect) in multi-turn conversations. From English WildChat dialogues [40] (≥6\geq 6 user turns), we annotate causal per-turn states offline, train a user simulator to generate utterances and ground-truth states sts_{t} (Appendix D.1), and form disjoint critic/SFT (3,0003{,}000), RL (3,5003{,}500), validation (200200), and test (500500) splits (Appendix B.2). Because conversational quality spans multiple axes that a single online scalar can misspecify, RL optimizes terminal belief-tracking accuracy (11–1010 rating rescaled to Rtask∈[0,1]R_{\text{task}}\in[0,1]; Appendix F.3), whereas test evaluation measures multi-axis agent utility in fresh closed-loop rollouts (T≤15T\leq 15). Specifically on the test dialogues, the frozen assistant sees only a local window (k=1k=1) with just the most recent turn (ut−1,at−1)(u_{t-1},a_{t-1}), the latest user message utu_{t}, and zt−1z_{t-1}. Given (u1:T,a1:T)(u_{1:T},a_{1:T}) and true states s0:Ts_{0:T}, GPT-4.1 rates (11–1010) Overall User Satisfaction, Goal Completion, Preference & Constraint Retention, and Coherence & Adaptability (Appendix D.4). Table 1 reports signed Δ\Delta vs. a memory-free No-Belief baseline (k=1k=1 only) on all N=500N=500 dialogues and on T≥10T\geq 10 dialogues (N=158N=158 seeds with ≥10\geq 10 turns under No-Belief).

Baselines and Implementation.

We compare MaxIM against three non-RL baselines: Prompt-Only (zero-shot base updates), Policy SFT (distilled on offline oracle summaries; Appendix B), and Best-of-NN MI SFT (N=8N=8 on arXiv; distilling single-step updates with highest shaping reward r^t\hat{r}_{t} to test myopic MI selection); two sparse-reward RL baselines: MemAgent RL [7] and Task-Only RL, which do not use MI shaping; and two ablations: Suff-Only RL (wc=0w_{c}=0, no recursive consistency) and MI-Only RL (Rtask=0R_{\text{task}}=0, shaping only). Summarizers, the unified critics, frozen actors, and the user simulator use Gemini 2.5 Flash [41]; offline summary target synthesis and the RL belief rater use Gemini 3.0 Flash; and test-time WildChat ratings, atomic-claim grounding, and qualitative evaluations use cross-family GPT-4.1. RL methods use G=8G=8 and γ=0.9\gamma=0.9 (γ=1.0\gamma=1.0 for MemAgent RL), with zero critic calls at test time.

5.2 Main Results: Downstream Task Utility and Budget Scaling (RQ1)

Scientific Reading and Long-Range Credit Assignment.

On arXiv (K=500K=500, Table 1), non-RL baselines abstain on 59%59\%–70%70\% of synthesis questions: Prompt-Only (31.30%31.30\%) lacks guidance on which details matter downstream, Policy SFT (38.76%38.76\%) compounds exposure bias over 2525 updates, and Best-of-NN MI SFT (29.05%29.05\%) confirms Corollary 1 (Appendix A.4)—greedily selecting single-step updates by immediate PMI cannot plan capacity across chunks or replace non-myopic RL. Sparse-reward RL substantially improves retention (MemAgent 52.90%52.90\%, Task-Only 54.44%54.44\%), yet MaxIM reaches 66.39%\mathbf{66.39\%}, beating Task-Only by +11.95\mathbf{+11.95} pp and MemAgent by +13.49\mathbf{+13.49} pp and cutting abstention to 32.0%32.0\%. On the Early-Section Stress Test (chunks 33–77), MaxIM’s lead widens to 48.55%\mathbf{48.55\%} vs. 32.23%32.23\% for Task-Only (+50.6%\mathbf{+50.6\%} relative) and 17.35%17.35\% for Prompt-Only, confirming dense PMI shaping helps retain early task-relevant details.

Token-Budget Pareto Frontier.

Across strict budgets K∈{100,300,500,800}K\in\{100,300,500,800\} (Figure 2(a)), MaxIM dominates the Pareto frontier: at K=100K=100, MaxIM achieves 34.26%\mathbf{34.26\%} Abstain-MCQ—beating Prompt-Only at a 5×5\times larger K=500K=500 budget (31.30%31.30\%)—and at K=500K=500 (66.39%66.39\%) it surpasses Prompt-Only even at K=2,000K=2{,}000 (64.32%64.32\%; Table 6), saturating smoothly at 67.04%67.04\% (K=800K=800) per Proposition 4. Figure 2(b) tracks chunk claim incorporation (the share of atomic claims in chunk oto_{t} entailed by ztz_{t}): all methods incorporate 45%45\%–50%50\% in chunks 11–55, but baselines saturate once the K=500K=500 buffer fills whereas MaxIM sustains 26.8%\mathbf{26.8\%} even in chunks 2121–2525.

Bounded-Memory Multi-Turn Dialogue: When Imperfect Beliefs Hurt.

On WildChat (Table 1), the assistant with no belief tracking (No-Belief) already scores high on average (8.588.58 Sat., 8.748.74 Pref.). However, its scores drop noticeably on longer dialogues (T≥10T\geq 10) to 8.088.08 and 8.288.28. Strikingly, every baseline without MI shaping underperforms No-Belief on Satisfaction and Goal Completion—including Task-Only RL (Δ=−0.30\Delta=-0.30, p=0.0084p=0.0084; −0.37-0.37 on T≥10T\geq 10) and MemAgent RL (Δ=−0.28\Delta=-0.28, p=0.0206p=0.0206): conditioning replies on inaccurately tracked beliefs steers the assistant toward false assumptions, proving worse than no belief state at all. Notably, Task-Only (8.79/108.79/10) and MemAgent (8.98/108.98/10) nearly match MaxIM (9.00/109.00/10; Table 10) on the terminal belief-tracking reward RtaskR_{\text{task}} itself; optimizing terminal belief accuracy alone fails to improve agent utility because it tolerates intermediate-turn hallucinations and omissions that derail live responses (Section 5.3).

Long-Horizon Recovery via MI Shaping. By contrast, on T≥10T\geq 10 dialogues, only MI-shaped policies outperform No-Belief across every metric (bottom block of Table 1). Full MaxIM is the only method with positive gains (Δ>0\Delta>0) across all metrics on both cohorts, hitting Δ=+0.30\Delta=\mathbf{+0.30} on T≥10T\geq 10 Preference Retention while resolving goals in fewer turns (10.6810.68 vs. 12.6112.61; Table 9), beating Task-Only by +0.35\mathbf{+0.35} Sat. (p=0.0012p=0.0012; +0.48\mathbf{+0.48} on T≥10T\geq 10) and MemAgent by +0.34\mathbf{+0.34} (p=0.0032p=0.0032).

5.3 Factual Grounding and Qualitative Assessment (RQ2)

GPT-4.1 evaluates two protocols (Table 2; Appendix E): atomic-claim grounding decomposes terminal zTz_{T} into claims classified against the source as supported (Entail %), neutral, or fabricated/distorted (Contr %), and reports mean supported claims (Gnd. Claims); qualitative evaluation compares each method vs. Prompt-Only (t=20t=20 on arXiv; zTz_{T} on WildChat) on task helpfulness (Use Win %) and faithfulness (Truth Win %), and scores arXiv Consistency (Cons.) on a 11–1010 scale by whether (zt−1,ot)→zt(z_{t-1},o_{t})\to z_{t} preserves prior context while integrating oto_{t}.

Factual Grounding and Qualitative Trade-Offs on Scientific Reading.

In Table 2 (left), RL policies sustain high arXiv entailment (97.5%97.5\%–98.4%98.4\%), whereas Policy SFT degrades (75.01%75.01\% entailment, 11.62%11.62\% contradiction) as errors compound across 2525 sequential updates. MaxIM attains 97.48%\mathbf{97.48\%} entailment while packing 54.0\mathbf{54.0} grounded claims—63.6%63.6\% above Prompt-Only (33.033.0) and above Task-Only (47.347.3) and MemAgent (47.647.6), whereas MI-Only packs 63.463.4 claims with low selectivity (47.0%47.0\% Usefulness). Against Prompt-Only at t=20t=20, MemAgent has a higher Usefulness win rate than MaxIM (80.1%80.1\% vs. 72.9%72.9\%), whereas MaxIM achieves the highest Consistency overall (7.55\mathbf{7.55} vs. MemAgent’s 6.076.07), retains more claims (54.054.0 vs. 47.647.6), and leads by 13.4913.49 pp on Abstain-MCQ. Moreover, when GPT-4.1 compares MaxIM and MemAgent directly (t=3​…​20t=3\dots 20), it prefers MaxIM on Usefulness at every chunk (54.8%54.8\%–72.0%72.0\% win rate; Table 11).

Dynamic Belief Grounding on WildChat.

While arXiv provides explicit text, WildChat requires inferring implicit user states without confabulation. MaxIM achieves the highest entailment (91.75%\mathbf{91.75\%}), cuts contradictions to 4.27%\mathbf{4.27\%}—𝟓𝟒%\mathbf{54\%} below MemAgent (9.35%9.35\%), 𝟑𝟗%\mathbf{39\%} below Task-Only (7.04%7.04\%), and 𝟔𝟏%\mathbf{61\%} below Prompt-Only (11.04%11.04\%)—and retains nearly twice as many grounded claims (40.340.3 vs. 21.021.0–23.123.1), explaining why MaxIM aids the k=1k=1 assistant while unshaped RL misleads it. MaxIM also leads Truthfulness (72.4%\mathbf{72.4\%}) and ranks second in Usefulness (73.8%73.8\% vs. Task-Only’s 79.8%79.8\%). Figure 2(c) (Table 11) shows why: for t≤5t\leq 5, Task-Only’s speculative inferences edge MaxIM on Usefulness (82.1%82.1\% vs. 79.5%79.5\% at t=5t=5) at lower Truthfulness (70.5%70.5\% vs. 78.6%\mathbf{78.6\%}), whereas for t≥8t\geq 8 MaxIM leads every baseline on both Usefulness (up to 90.2%\mathbf{90.2\%}) and Truthfulness (88.5%\mathbf{88.5\%}).

5.4 Ablation Studies: Reward Components and Annealing Dynamics (RQ3)

Synergy of Sufficiency, Recursive Consistency, and Task Anchoring.

Table 3(a) isolates each reward term: only full MaxIM achieves positive WildChat Δ\Delta Sat. (+0.05+0.05; +0.23+0.23 vs. Suff-Only, +0.35+0.35 vs. Task-Only). Dropping recursive consistency (Suff-Only RL, wc=0w_{c}=0) cuts arXiv accuracy by −14.85-14.85 pp (51.54%51.54\%), yields the lowest consistency (5.995.99; Table 2), and raises WildChat contradictions by +51.8%+51.8\% (6.48%6.48\% vs. 4.27%4.27\%): while Suff-Only aids T≥10T\geq 10 dialogues (Δ=+0.16\Delta=+0.16; Table 1), unregularized sufficiency rewards speculative claims (Lemma 1) that pull overall Satisfaction negative (Δ=−0.18\Delta=-0.18, p=0.048p=0.048). Conversely, MI-Only RL (Rtask=0R_{\text{task}}=0) reaches 50.30%50.30\% arXiv accuracy and +0.18+0.18 T≥10T\geq 10 Satisfaction without task reward (Proposition 1), yet leaves a 16.0916.09 pp arXiv gap and 10.53%10.53\% contradictions (Proposition 6(ii)), motivating task anchoring.

Role of Mid-Training Cosine Annealing.

Table 3(b) varies the λs\lambda_{s} decay window on arXiv (K=500K=500). Constant shaping (No Annealing, 57.10%57.10\%) beats Task-Only (54.44%54.44\%), while decaying too early (13%13\%–60%60\%, 61.18%61.18\%) or late (65%65\%–90%90\%, 61.12%61.12\%) trails Mid-Decay (45%45\%–60%60\%, 66.39%\mathbf{66.39\%}) by >5>5 pp (+9.29\mathbf{+9.29} pp over none). Holding λs=1\lambda_{s}=1 early guides exploration toward informative, grounded summaries (escaping sparse-reward plateaus), while mid-training decay (λs→0\lambda_{s}\to 0) lets late updates optimize RtaskR_{\text{task}} without critic bias (Proposition 6(iii)).

6 Conclusion

In this work, we introduced MaxIM, a mathematically principled RL framework for capacity-constrained incremental summarization. To overcome the severe credit assignment bottlenecks of sparse, long-horizon task rewards, we formulated context compression as an information-theoretic reward shaping problem. By establishing formal links between value suboptimality and sequential information loss across static and dynamic POMDPs, we derived two complementary, dense regularizers: predictive sufficiency to promote downstream task utility, and recursive consistency to enforce factual grounding and substantially reduce LLM hallucination. By exploiting a unified asymmetric critic architecture trained on scalable synthetic data with PMI scoring and no test-time overhead, MaxIM provides dense step-wise shaping signals without a need for expensive human preference labels. Our empirical evaluations across long-horizon scientific reading and closed-loop multi-turn conversation settings demonstrate that MaxIM achieves superior downstream task success, Pareto-efficient token compression, and factual consistency.

Appendix A Theoretical Analysis and Proofs

This appendix presents the unified formal analysis and complete proofs for all theoretical claims in Section 4: Theorem 1 and Proposition 3 on POMDPs with static or action-dependent targets (Appendix A.1); Propositions 1 and 4 on predictive sufficiency, finite-KK rate-distortion floors, and critic posterior approximation error (Appendix A.2); Lemma 1 on the hallucination failure mode (Appendix A.3); Propositions 2 and 5 together with Corollary 1 on recursive consistency, sequential information loss under local context updates, and non-myopic RL (Appendix A.4); and Proposition 6 on pointwise mutual information (PMI) identities and critic distribution shift under KL-regularized RL and annealing (Appendix A.5).

A.1 Proof of Theorem 1 and Approximate Target Mediation

Let μθ\mu_{\theta} denote the trajectory distribution induced by rolling out the incremental summarizer πθ​(zt∣zt−1,at−1,ot)\pi_{\theta}(z_{t}\mid z_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t}) alongside the fixed downstream action agent πact​(at∣zt,ot)\pi_{\text{act}}(a_{t}\mid z_{t},o_{t}). Denote the full-history posterior belief by bt(⋅)≔P(Yt∈⋅∣Ht)b_{t}(\cdot)\coloneqq P(Y_{t}\in\cdot\mid H_{t}) and the compressed posterior belief by b^t(⋅)≔P(Yt∈⋅∣zt)\hat{b}_{t}(\cdot)\coloneqq P(Y_{t}\in\cdot\mid z_{t}). Formally, V∗​(Ht)≔supπ~act𝔼⁡[∑k≥tγk−t​Rtask,k∣Ht]V^{*}(H_{t})\coloneqq\sup_{\tilde{\pi}_{\text{act}}}\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_{k\geq t}\gamma^{k-t}R_{\text{task},k}\mid H_{t}\big] denotes the optimal value achievable over history-measurable actor policies π~act​(ak∣Hk)\tilde{\pi}_{\text{act}}(a_{k}\mid H_{k}), and V∗​(zt)≔supπact𝔼πθ​[∑k≥tγk−t​Rtask,k∣zt]V^{*}(z_{t})\coloneqq\sup_{\pi_{\text{act}}}\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}\big[\sum_{k\geq t}\gamma^{k-t}R_{\text{task},k}\mid z_{t}\big] denotes the optimal value over (zk,ok)(z_{k},o_{k})-measurable actor policies πact​(ak∣zk,ok)\pi_{\text{act}}(a_{k}\mid z_{k},o_{k}) holding the summarizer kernel πθ\pi_{\theta} fixed. Assumptions (A1)–(A3) in Section 4.1 state:

  1. (A1)

    Target Mediation: There exist transition and observation kernels T,OT,O and an expected reward function r:𝒴×𝒜→[−Rmax,Rmax]r:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{A}\to[-R_{\max},R_{\max}] such that conditionally on (Ht,Yt,at)(H_{t},Y_{t},a_{t}), Yt+1∼T(⋅∣Yt,at)Y_{t+1}\sim T(\cdot\mid Y_{t},a_{t}), ot+1∼O(⋅∣Yt+1,at)o_{t+1}\sim O(\cdot\mid Y_{t+1},a_{t}), and 𝔼[Rtask,t∣Ht,at]=⟨bt,r(⋅,at)⟩\mathbb{E}[R_{\text{task},t}\mid H_{t},a_{t}]=\langle b_{t},r(\cdot,a_{t})\rangle. This subsumes both passive document reading (T(⋅∣y,a)=δyT(\cdot\mid y,a)=\delta_{y}, as in arXiv) and interactive closed-loop POMDPs where actions ata_{t} alter future latent states Yt+1Y_{t+1} (as in WildChat).

  2. (A2)

    Memory Causality: zt⟂Yt|Htz_{t}\perp Y_{t}\mid H_{t}, since πθ\pi_{\theta} conditions only on (zt−1,at−1,ot)⊆Ht(z_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t})\subseteq H_{t} and exogenous sampling randomness (privileged targets YtY_{t} are accessed solely by the offline critic during training).

  3. (A3)

    Compressed Acting: at⟂Yt|(Ht,zt)a_{t}\perp Y_{t}\mid(H_{t},z_{t}), which holds whenever at∼πact(⋅∣zt,ot)a_{t}\sim\pi_{\text{act}}(\cdot\mid z_{t},o_{t}) (or conditioned additionally on bounded recent turns) uses exogenous randomness.

Theorem 1 (Value Suboptimality Bound; extending [33, 34]). Let V∗​(Ht)V^{*}(H_{t}) be the optimal expected return achievable with the full observation history, and V∗​(zt)V^{*}(z_{t}) be the optimal expected return achievable using the capacity-constrained summary ztz_{t}. Under Assumptions (A1)–(A3) with rewards bounded in [−Rmax,Rmax][-R_{\max},R_{\max}], the expected suboptimality gap under the induced trajectory distribution μθ\mu_{\theta} is bounded by the sequential information loss Iμθ​(Yt;Ht∣zt)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t}):

𝔼μθ​[|V∗​(Ht)−V∗​(zt)|]≤2​Rmax(1−γ)2​supkIμθ​(Yk;Hk∣zk),\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\theta}}\big[|V^{*}(H_{t})-V^{*}(z_{t})|\big]\leq\frac{\sqrt{2}R_{\max}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\sqrt{\sup_{k}I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{k};H_{k}\mid z_{k})},

and conditioning on closed-loop actions never inflates this loss: Iμθ(Yt;Ht∣zt,at)≤Iμθ(Yt;Ht∣zt)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t},a_{t})\leq I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t}).

Proof.

From the agent’s perspective, mapping the true observation history HtH_{t} into a capacity-constrained summary ztz_{t} acts as a lossy state abstraction. Operating on this abstraction introduces approximation errors in predicting both the immediate reward and the transition dynamics. By the performance difference bounds for state abstractions (e.g., Theorem 2 in [33] and approximate information state Bellman induction [34]), the value suboptimality is bounded by the maximum single-step Bellman error ϵt\epsilon_{t} introduced by the abstraction, multiplied by 11−γ\frac{1}{1-\gamma}. This error ϵt\epsilon_{t} is bounded by the sum of immediate reward errors (Δ​Rt\Delta R_{t}) and discounted transition dynamics errors (γ​Δ​Pt⋅Vmax\gamma\Delta P_{t}\cdot V_{\max}).

Crucially, we evaluate both Bellman operators at each common fixed action a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, so exogeneity or marginal stationarity of YtY_{t} is never required. By (A2), P(Yt∈⋅∣Ht,zt)=btP(Y_{t}\in\cdot\mid H_{t},z_{t})=b_{t} almost surely. Because the immediate reward function depends strictly on the target variable YtY_{t} via (A1), the maximum single-step reward error Δ​Rt\Delta R_{t} is bounded by the Total Variation (TV) distance between the true posterior belief bt=P⁡(Yt∣Ht)b_{t}=P(Y_{t}\mid H_{t}) and the compressed posterior belief b^t=P⁡(Yt∣zt)\hat{b}_{t}=P(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}):

Δ​Rt=supa∈𝒜|⟨bt−b^t,r⁡(⋅,a)⟩|≤(max⁡R−min⁡R)⋅DTV​(P⁡(Yt∣Ht),P⁡(Yt∣zt))=2​Rmax⋅DTV.\Delta R_{t}=\sup_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\big|\langle b_{t}-\hat{b}_{t},r(\cdot,a)\rangle\big|\leq(\max R-\min R)\cdot D_{\mathrm{TV}}\big(P(Y_{t}\mid H_{t}),P(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})\big)=2R_{\max}\cdot D_{\mathrm{TV}}. (8)

For the transition dynamics error Δ​Pt\Delta P_{t}, standard abstraction proofs evaluate the divergence in the environment’s transition model for a fixed action. In static environments, the underlying state does not evolve, so Δ​Pt=0\Delta P_{t}=0. In dynamic closed-loop environments, for any fixed action a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, define the fixed-action Markov kernel Ga(y,⋅)≔∫𝒴O(⋅∣y′,a)T(dy′∣y,a)G_{a}(y,\cdot)\coloneqq\int_{\mathcal{Y}}O(\cdot\mid y^{\prime},a)\,T(\mathrm{d}y^{\prime}\mid y,a) mapping current latent states to next observations. Under (A1)–(A2), the full-history and compressed next-observation laws at action aa are linear pushforwards ⟨bt,Ga⟩\langle b_{t},G_{a}\rangle and ⟨b^t,Ga⟩\langle\hat{b}_{t},G_{a}\rangle; because both operators evaluate the identical action aa through the shared kernel GaG_{a}, the causal effect of aa on Yt+1Y_{t+1} enters both sides identically, and data processing for TV yields DTV​(⟨bt,Ga⟩,⟨b^t,Ga⟩)≤DTV​(bt,b^t)D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\langle b_{t},G_{a}\rangle,\langle\hat{b}_{t},G_{a}\rangle)\leq D_{\mathrm{TV}}(b_{t},\hat{b}_{t}) (preserved under composition with πθ​(zt+1∣zt,a,ot+1)\pi_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid z_{t},a,o_{t+1})). Accounting for dual-signed value differences in [−Vmax,Vmax][-V_{\max},V_{\max}] gives |𝔼[V∗(Ht+1)∣Ht,a]−𝔼[V∗(zt+1)∣zt,a]||\mathbb{E}[V^{*}(H_{t+1})\mid H_{t},a]-\mathbb{E}[V^{*}(z_{t+1})\mid z_{t},a]| residual contribution bounded via Δ​Pt⋅Vmax≤2​DTV⋅Vmax\Delta P_{t}\cdot V_{\max}\leq 2D_{\mathrm{TV}}\cdot V_{\max}.

Let Vmax≤Rmax1−γV_{\max}\leq\frac{R_{\max}}{1-\gamma} be the maximum possible value achievable. The worst-case single-step Bellman error ϵt\epsilon_{t} is bounded by:

ϵt≤Δ​Rt+γ​Δ​Pt⋅Vmax≤2​Rmax1−γ​DTV.\epsilon_{t}\leq\Delta R_{t}+\gamma\Delta P_{t}\cdot V_{\max}\leq\frac{2R_{\max}}{1-\gamma}D_{\mathrm{TV}}. (9)

By Pinsker’s inequality, the TV distance is bounded by the KL divergence: DTV≤12​DKLD_{\mathrm{TV}}\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}}. Substituting this yields:

ϵt≤2​Rmax1−γ​DKL(P(Yt∣Ht)∥P(Yt∣zt)).\epsilon_{t}\leq\frac{\sqrt{2}R_{\max}}{1-\gamma}\sqrt{D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(P(Y_{t}\mid H_{t})\,\|\,P(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})\big)}. (10)

We now take the expectation over the induced trajectory distribution μθ\mu_{\theta}. By Jensen’s Inequality (𝔼⁡[X]≤𝔼⁡[X]\mathbb{E}[\sqrt{X}]\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[X]}):

𝔼μθ​[ϵt]≤2​Rmax1−γ​𝔼μθ​[DKL]≤2​Rmax1−γ​𝔼μθ​[DKL].\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\theta}}[\epsilon_{t}]\leq\frac{\sqrt{2}R_{\max}}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\theta}}\!\left[\sqrt{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\right]\leq\frac{\sqrt{2}R_{\max}}{1-\gamma}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\theta}}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}]}. (11)

By (A2), the expected KL divergence between the true and compressed conditionals over the joint distribution is precisely the conditional mutual information, or information loss:

𝔼μθ[DKL(P(Yt∣Ht)∥P(Yt∣zt))]=Iμθ(Yt;Ht∣zt).\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\theta}}\big[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P(Y_{t}\mid H_{t})\,\|\,P(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}))\big]=I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t}). (12)

Summing this step-wise bound across the discounted horizon (∑k≥tγk−t=11−γ\sum_{k\geq t}\gamma^{k-t}=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}) yields Eq. (2). Finally, expanding Iμθ​(Yt;(Ht,at)∣zt)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};(H_{t},a_{t})\mid z_{t}) in both orders gives Iμθ(Yt;Ht∣zt)+Iμθ(Yt;at∣Ht,zt)=Iμθ(Yt;at∣zt)+Iμθ(Yt;Ht∣zt,at)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t})+I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};a_{t}\mid H_{t},z_{t})=I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};a_{t}\mid z_{t})+I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t},a_{t}); since Iμθ(Yt;at∣Ht,zt)=0I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};a_{t}\mid H_{t},z_{t})=0 by (A3) and Iμθ​(Yt;at∣zt)≥0I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};a_{t}\mid z_{t})\geq 0, we obtain Iμθ(Yt;Ht∣zt,at)≤Iμθ(Yt;Ht∣zt)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t},a_{t})\leq I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t}). ∎

Proposition 3 (Approximate Target Mediation).

If Assumption (A1) holds only approximately—with reward mediation error supHt,a|𝔼[Rtask,t∣Ht,a]−⟨bt,r(⋅,a)⟩|≤εr\sup_{H_{t},a}|\mathbb{E}[R_{\text{task},t}\mid H_{t},a]-\langle b_{t},r(\cdot,a)\rangle|\leq\varepsilon_{r} and observation kernel error supHt,aDTV​(P⁡(ot+1∣Ht,a),⟨bt,Ga⟩)≤εT\sup_{H_{t},a}D_{\mathrm{TV}}(P(o_{t+1}\mid H_{t},a),\langle b_{t},G_{a}\rangle)\leq\varepsilon_{T}—then Theorem 1 holds with an explicit additive misspecification floor +2​εr+2​γ​Vmax​εT1−γ+\frac{2\varepsilon_{r}+2\gamma V_{\max}\varepsilon_{T}}{1-\gamma}.

Proof.

Applying the triangle inequality to Eqs. (8)–(9) adds 2​εr+2​γ​Vmax​εT2\varepsilon_{r}+2\gamma V_{\max}\varepsilon_{T} to each per-step Bellman residual, which accumulates across ∑k≥tγk−t=(1−γ)−1\sum_{k\geq t}\gamma^{k-t}=(1-\gamma)^{-1} to +2​εr+2​γ​Vmax​εT1−γ+\frac{2\varepsilon_{r}+2\gamma V_{\max}\varepsilon_{T}}{1-\gamma}. ∎

A.2 Proof of Proposition 1 and Capacity / Critic-Transfer Bounds

Proof of Proposition 1.

By definition, the conditional mutual information expands as:

Iμθ​(Yt;Ht∣zt)=Hμθ​(Yt∣zt)−Hμθ​(Yt∣Ht,zt).I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t})=H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid H_{t},z_{t}). (13)

Because the summary ztz_{t} is generated solely by conditioning on the history HtH_{t} (Assumption (A2)), they form the Markov chain Yt→Ht→ztY_{t}\to H_{t}\to z_{t}, yielding Hμθ​(Yt∣Ht,zt)=Hμθ​(Yt∣Ht)H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid H_{t},z_{t})=H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid H_{t}) and hence:

Iμθ​(Yt;Ht∣zt)=Hμθ​(Yt∣zt)−Hμθ​(Yt∣Ht).I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t})=H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid H_{t}). (14)

The term Hμθ​(Yt∣Ht)H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid H_{t}) represents the irreducible uncertainty of the target given the full history. Introducing a parameterized variational distribution qϕ​(Yt∣zt)q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}), the expected variational log-likelihood satisfies the exact identity:

𝔼μθ​[log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣zt)]=−Hμθ​(Yt∣zt)⏟predictive sufficiency−𝔼zt∼μθ[DKL(Pμθ(Yt∣zt)∥qϕ(Yt∣zt))]⏟≕Δpost​(ϕ,θ)≥ 0.\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\theta}}[\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})]=\underbrace{-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})}_{\text{predictive sufficiency}}-\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{z_{t}\sim\mu_{\theta}}\!\Big[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(P_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})\,\|\,q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})\big)\Big]}_{\eqqcolon\,\Delta_{\mathrm{post}}(\phi;\theta)\,\geq\,0}. (15)

Thus 𝔼μθ​[log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣zt)]≤−Hμθ​(Yt∣zt)\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\theta}}[\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})]\leq-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}) is a variational lower bound on predictive sufficiency, and substituting Eq. (15) into Eq. (14) gives Iμθ​(Yt;Ht∣zt)=𝔼μθ​[−log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣zt)]−Hμθ​(Yt∣Ht)−Δpost​(ϕ,θ)≤𝔼μθ​[−log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣zt)]−Hμθ​(Yt∣Ht)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\theta}}[-\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})]-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid H_{t})-\Delta_{\mathrm{post}}(\phi;\theta)\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\theta}}[-\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})]-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid H_{t}), bypassing any assumption of constant marginal entropy Hμθ​(Yt)H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}). ∎

Intuition and Interpretation of Proposition 4.

Before stating Proposition 4, we highlight its two practical takeaways. First, in practice ztz_{t} is limited to KK discrete tokens, so zero information loss is unattainable whenever HtH_{t} contains more than K​log⁡|𝒱|+log⁡2K\log|\mathcal{V}|+\log 2 nats of task-relevant signal about YtY_{t}: Part (i) shows that optimal information loss obeys a rate-distortion floor ιt​(K)\iota_{t}(K) that decreases at most linearly with budget KK and saturates at 00 once KK can encode a minimal sufficient statistic for YtY_{t}—directly explaining the concave budget-scaling curve in Figure 2(a). Second, RL optimizes a learned offline critic qϕq_{\phi} rather than the unknown true posterior Pμθ​(Yt∣zt)P_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}): Part (ii) shows that optimizing the discounted variational surrogate transfers directly into a downstream value guarantee up to critic posterior error Δ¯\bar{\Delta} (decomposed in Eq. (18) into critic capacity, finite-sample fit, and distribution shift), optimization tolerance δ\delta, and closed-loop filtering variation Δfilt\Delta_{\mathrm{filt}} (Δfilt=0\Delta_{\mathrm{filt}}=0 on static tasks such as arXiv).

Proposition 4 (Finite-KK Capacity Floor and Approximate-Critic Transfer).

Under Assumptions (A1)–(A3) with token budget zt∈𝒵K≔⋃ℓ=0K𝒱ℓz_{t}\in\mathcal{Z}_{K}\coloneqq\bigcup_{\ell=0}^{K}\mathcal{V}^{\ell} (|𝒱|≥2|\mathcal{V}|\geq 2) over feasible policy class ΘK\Theta_{K}:

  1. (i)

    Finite-KK Rate-Distortion Floor: Define ιt​(K)≔infπθ∈ΘKIμθ​(Yt;Ht∣zt)\iota_{t}(K)\coloneqq\inf_{\pi_{\theta}\in\Theta_{K}}I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t}). Then Iμθ​(Yt;Ht∣zt)=Iμθ​(Yt,Ht)−Iμθ​(Yt,zt)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t})=I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t})-I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};z_{t}), and

    ιt​(K)≥max⁡{0,infπθ∈ΘKIμθ​(Yt,Ht)−K​log⁡|𝒱|−log⁡2}.\iota_{t}(K)\geq\max\Big\{0,\,\inf_{\pi_{\theta}\in\Theta_{K}}I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t})-K\log|\mathcal{V}|-\log 2\Big\}. (16)
  2. (ii)

    Approximate-Critic Value Transfer: Define the discounted variational objective J¯surr,t​(θ)≔(1−γ)​∑k≥tγk−t​𝔼μθ​[log⁡qϕ​(Yk∣zk)]\bar{J}_{\mathrm{surr},t}(\theta)\coloneqq(1-\gamma)\sum_{k\geq t}\gamma^{k-t}\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\theta}}[\log q_{\phi}(Y_{k}\mid z_{k})] and discounted capacity floor ι¯t​(K)≔infπθ∈ΘK(1−γ)​∑k≥tγk−t​Iμθ​(Yk;Hk∣zk)≥(1−γ)​∑k≥tγk−t​ιk​(K)\bar{\iota}_{t}(K)\coloneqq\inf_{\pi_{\theta}\in\Theta_{K}}(1-\gamma)\sum_{k\geq t}\gamma^{k-t}I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{k};H_{k}\mid z_{k})\geq(1-\gamma)\sum_{k\geq t}\gamma^{k-t}\iota_{k}(K). Let Δ¯≔supk≥tsupθ∈ΘKΔpost,k​(ϕ,θ)\bar{\Delta}\coloneqq\sup_{k\geq t}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{K}}\Delta_{\mathrm{post},k}(\phi;\theta) bound the critic posterior gap and Δfilt≔supk≥tsupθ,θ′∈ΘK|Hμθ​(Yk∣Hk)−Hμθ′​(Yk∣Hk)|\Delta_{\mathrm{filt}}\coloneqq\sup_{k\geq t}\sup_{\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\Theta_{K}}\big|H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{k}\mid H_{k})-H_{\mu_{\theta^{\prime}}}(Y_{k}\mid H_{k})\big| bound closed-loop filtering-entropy variation (Δfilt=0\Delta_{\mathrm{filt}}=0 identically for static/exogenous targets). Then any δ\delta-approximate maximizer θ^∈ΘK\hat{\theta}\in\Theta_{K} satisfying J¯surr,t​(θ^)≥supθ∈ΘKJ¯surr,t​(θ)−δ\bar{J}_{\mathrm{surr},t}(\hat{\theta})\geq\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{K}}\bar{J}_{\mathrm{surr},t}(\theta)-\delta obeys

+(B+log⁡|𝒴|)​DTV​(νθ,ν𝒟)+h⁡(DTV​(νθ,ν𝒟))⏟Δshift​(θ).\displaystyle+\underbrace{\big(B+\log|\mathcal{Y}|\big)D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\nu_{\theta},\nu_{\mathcal{D}})+h\!\big(D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\nu_{\theta},\nu_{\mathcal{D}})\big)}_{\Delta_{\mathrm{shift}}(\theta)}.

A.3 Justification of Lemma 1 (The Hallucination Failure Mode)

Justification.

We show that optimizing solely for predictive sufficiency, maxθ⁡[−Hμθ​(Yt∣zt)]\max_{\theta}[-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})], leaves the policy vulnerable to hallucination because natural language is expressive and over-parameterized relative to a sparse target.

By the Data Processing Inequality (DPI) applied to the Markov chain Yt→Ht→ztY_{t}\to H_{t}\to z_{t}, Iμθ​(zt,Ht)≥Iμθ​(zt,Yt)=Hμθ​(Yt)−Hμθ​(Yt∣zt)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t};H_{t})\geq I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t};Y_{t})=H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t})-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}), so a nonzero minimum amount of historical signal is needed to achieve high predictive sufficiency −Hμθ​(Yt∣zt)-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}). However, when H⁡(Yt)≪K​log⁡|𝒱|H(Y_{t})\ll K\log|\mathcal{V}|, encoding YtY_{t} consumes only a fraction of the KK-token budget, leaving many distinct strings ztz_{t} that induce the exact same posterior P⁡(Yt∣zt)P(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}). Under KL-regularized RL anchored to a pre-trained LLM prior πpre\pi_{\text{pre}}, an unconstrained policy fills residual capacity with fluent, high-prior-probability continuations correlated with YtY_{t} rather than grounded exclusively in HtH_{t}.

Concretely, suppose ztz_{t} decomposes bijectively into task-relevant semantics ztYz_{t}^{Y} extracted from HtH_{t} and auxiliary narrative ztnoisez_{t}^{\text{noise}} sampled conditionally on ztYz_{t}^{Y} independently of (Ht,Yt)(H_{t},Y_{t}), so ztnoise⟂(Ht,Yt)|ztYz_{t}^{\text{noise}}\perp(H_{t},Y_{t})\mid z_{t}^{Y}. Then predictive sufficiency is completely unchanged, −Hμθ​(Yt∣ztY,ztnoise)=−Hμθ​(Yt∣ztY)-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}^{Y},z_{t}^{\text{noise}})=-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}^{Y}), while the chain rule of mutual information gives

Iμθ​(zt,Ht)=Iμθ​(ztY,Ht)+Iμθ​(ztnoise;Ht∣ztY)=Iμθ​(ztY,Ht),I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t};H_{t})=I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}^{Y};H_{t})+I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}^{\text{noise}};H_{t}\mid z_{t}^{Y})=I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}^{Y};H_{t}), (19)

suppressing historical mutual information to the bare minimum needed for ztYz_{t}^{Y} while inflating ungrounded conditional entropy Hμθ​(zt∣Ht)=Hμθ​(ztY∣Ht)+Hμθ​(ztnoise∣ztY)H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}\mid H_{t})=H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}^{Y}\mid H_{t})+H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}^{\text{noise}}\mid z_{t}^{Y}) by the full entropy of the fabricated narrative ztnoisez_{t}^{\text{noise}}. ∎

A.4 Formalization and Proof of Proposition 2 and Recursive Sequential Information Loss

Proposition 2 (Formalized: Recursive Consistency Bounds Ungrounded Generation). Let πθ​(zt∣H~t)\pi_{\theta}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t}) map local context H~t=(zt−1,at−1,ot)\tilde{H}_{t}=(z_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t}) to bounded summaries 𝒵K≔⋃ℓ=0K𝒱ℓ\mathcal{Z}_{K}\coloneqq\bigcup_{\ell=0}^{K}\mathcal{V}^{\ell} (|𝒱|≥2|\mathcal{V}|\geq 2) with predictive sufficiency −Hμθ​(Yt∣zt)≥−η-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})\geq-\eta. Then:

  1. (i)

    Non-Degenerate Conditional Entropy Bound: Marginal summary entropy is bounded below away from collapse by Hμθ​(zt)≥Hμθ​(Yt)−ηH_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t})\geq H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t})-\eta, while conditional generation entropy satisfies

    Hμθ​(zt∣H~t)=Hμθ​(zt)−Iμθ​(zt,H~t)≤K​log⁡|𝒱|+log⁡2−Iμθ​(zt,H~t).H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t})=H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t})-I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t})\leq K\log|\mathcal{V}|+\log 2-I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t}). (20)

    In particular, for any decomposition zt↔(ztgnd,ztnoise)z_{t}\leftrightarrow(z_{t}^{\mathrm{gnd}},z_{t}^{\mathrm{noise}}) with ungrounded component ztnoise⟂H~t|ztgndz_{t}^{\mathrm{noise}}\perp\tilde{H}_{t}\mid z_{t}^{\mathrm{gnd}} (Lemma 1), Hμθ​(ztnoise∣ztgnd)≤K​log⁡|𝒱|+log⁡2−Iμθ​(zt,H~t)H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}^{\mathrm{noise}}\mid z_{t}^{\mathrm{gnd}})\leq K\log|\mathcal{V}|+\log 2-I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t}).

  2. (ii)

    Prior-Confabulation Rate Bound: If at context H~t\tilde{H}_{t} the policy samples from any history-independent confabulation prior Q∈Δ⁡(𝒵K)Q\in\Delta(\mathcal{Z}_{K}) with probability α⁡(H~t)∈[0,1]\alpha(\tilde{H}_{t})\in[0,1]—i.e., πθ(⋅∣H~t)=(1−α(H~t))πgnd(⋅∣H~t)+α(H~t)Q(⋅)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\tilde{H}_{t})=(1-\alpha(\tilde{H}_{t}))\pi_{\mathrm{gnd}}(\cdot\mid\tilde{H}_{t})+\alpha(\tilde{H}_{t})Q(\cdot)—then the expected confabulation rate α¯≔𝔼μθ​[α⁡(H~t)]\bar{\alpha}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\theta}}[\alpha(\tilde{H}_{t})] satisfies

    α¯≤1−Iμθ​(zt,H~t)−h⁡(α¯)K​log⁡|𝒱|+log⁡2≤1−Iμθ​(zt,H~t)−log⁡2K​log⁡|𝒱|+log⁡2,\bar{\alpha}\leq 1-\frac{I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t})-h(\bar{\alpha})}{K\log|\mathcal{V}|+\log 2}\leq 1-\frac{I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t})-\log 2}{K\log|\mathcal{V}|+\log 2}, (21)

    where h⁡(p)=−p​log⁡p−(1−p)​log⁡(1−p)h(p)=-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p) (and h⁡(α¯)h(\bar{\alpha}) is replaced by 00 when α⁡(H~t)≡α¯\alpha(\tilde{H}_{t})\equiv\bar{\alpha} is constant).

Proof.

Part (i): For discrete zt∈𝒵Kz_{t}\in\mathcal{Z}_{K}, Hμθ​(zt∣Yt)≥0H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}\mid Y_{t})\geq 0 implies Hμθ​(zt)≥Iμθ​(Yt,zt)=Hμθ​(Yt)−Hμθ​(Yt∣zt)≥Hμθ​(Yt)−ηH_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t})\geq I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};z_{t})=H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t})-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t})\geq H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t})-\eta, preventing collapse into context-independent low-entropy strings whenever Hμθ​(Yt)>ηH_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t})>\eta. Meanwhile |𝒵K|=∑ℓ=0K|𝒱|ℓ≤2​|𝒱|K|\mathcal{Z}_{K}|=\sum_{\ell=0}^{K}|\mathcal{V}|^{\ell}\leq 2|\mathcal{V}|^{K} yields Hμθ​(zt)≤K​log⁡|𝒱|+log⁡2H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t})\leq K\log|\mathcal{V}|+\log 2 and Eq. (20). Notice this is an upper-bound regularizer rather than an equivalence: maximizing Iμθ​(zt,H~t)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t}) forces Hμθ​(zt∣H~t)H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t}) down when capacity is utilized, and under zt↔(ztgnd,ztnoise)z_{t}\leftrightarrow(z_{t}^{\mathrm{gnd}},z_{t}^{\mathrm{noise}}) with ztnoise⟂H~t|ztgndz_{t}^{\mathrm{noise}}\perp\tilde{H}_{t}\mid z_{t}^{\mathrm{gnd}}, the chain rule gives Hμθ​(zt∣H~t)=Hμθ​(ztgnd∣H~t)+Hμθ​(ztnoise∣ztgnd)≥Hμθ​(ztnoise∣ztgnd)H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t})=H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}^{\mathrm{gnd}}\mid\tilde{H}_{t})+H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}^{\mathrm{noise}}\mid z_{t}^{\mathrm{gnd}})\geq H_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t}^{\mathrm{noise}}\mid z_{t}^{\mathrm{gnd}}).

By monotonicity and the chain rule of mutual information, Iμθ​(zt,H~t)≤I⁡(zt,U,H~t)=I⁡(U,H~t)+(1−α¯)​I​(zt;H~t∣U=0)+α¯​I​(zt;H~t∣U=1)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t})\leq I(z_{t},U;\tilde{H}_{t})=I(U;\tilde{H}_{t})+(1-\bar{\alpha})I(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t}\mid U=0)+\bar{\alpha}\,I(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t}\mid U=1). Since zt⟂H~t|(U=1)z_{t}\perp\tilde{H}_{t}\mid(U=1), I⁡(zt;H~t∣U=1)=0I(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t}\mid U=1)=0; on U=0U=0, I⁡(zt;H~t∣U=0)≤H⁡(zt∣U=0)≤K​log|𝒱|+log⁡2I(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t}\mid U=0)\leq H(z_{t}\mid U=0)\leq K\log|\mathcal{V}|+\log 2; and I⁡(U,H~t)≤H⁡(U)=h⁡(α¯)≤log⁡2I(U;\tilde{H}_{t})\leq H(U)=h(\bar{\alpha})\leq\log 2 (with I⁡(U,H~t)=0I(U;\tilde{H}_{t})=0 if α⁡(H~t)≡α¯\alpha(\tilde{H}_{t})\equiv\bar{\alpha}). Rearranging Iμθ​(zt,H~t)≤h⁡(α¯)+(1−α¯)​(K​log⁡|𝒱|+log⁡2)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t})\leq h(\bar{\alpha})+(1-\bar{\alpha})(K\log|\mathcal{V}|+\log 2) yields Eq. (21). ∎

Proposition 5 (Sequential Information Loss Under Recursive Updates).

Suppose πθ​(zt∣H~t)\pi_{\theta}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t}) updates memory solely from the local context H~t=(zt−1,at−1,ot)\tilde{H}_{t}=(z_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t}) (with H0=∅H_{0}=\varnothing). Then at every turn t≥1t\geq 1:

Iμθ​(Yt;Ht∣zt)=Iμθ​(Yt;H~t∣zt)+Iμθ​(Yt;Ht−1∣H~t).I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t})=I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};\tilde{H}_{t}\mid z_{t})+I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t-1}\mid\tilde{H}_{t}). (22)

Proof.

Because (Ht−1,H~t)=(Ht,zt−1)(H_{t-1},\tilde{H}_{t})=(H_{t},z_{t-1}) and zt−1⟂Yt|Htz_{t-1}\perp Y_{t}\mid H_{t} (as zt−1z_{t-1} is generated causally from Ht−1⊆HtH_{t-1}\subseteq H_{t} and private randomness), Iμθ​(Yt;Ht∣zt)=Iμθ​(Yt;(Ht−1,H~t)∣zt)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t}\mid z_{t})=I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};(H_{t-1},\tilde{H}_{t})\mid z_{t}). Expanding the right-hand side via the chain rule yields Iμθ(Yt;H~t∣zt)+Iμθ(Yt;Ht−1∣H~t,zt)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};\tilde{H}_{t}\mid z_{t})+I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t-1}\mid\tilde{H}_{t},z_{t}), and since zt⟂(Yt,Ht−1)|H~tz_{t}\perp(Y_{t},H_{t-1})\mid\tilde{H}_{t}, Iμθ(Yt;Ht−1∣H~t,zt)=Iμθ(Yt;Ht−1∣H~t)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t-1}\mid\tilde{H}_{t},z_{t})=I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t-1}\mid\tilde{H}_{t}), proving Eq. (22). Next, at t=1t=1, H0=∅H_{0}=\varnothing gives Iμθ​(Y1;H0∣H~1)=0I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{1};H_{0}\mid\tilde{H}_{1})=0. For t≥2t\geq 2, non-negativity of MI and the chain rule give Iμθ(Yt;Ht−1∣zt−1,at−1,ot)≤Iμθ((Yt,ot);Ht−1∣zt−1,at−1)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t};H_{t-1}\mid z_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t})\leq I_{\mu_{\theta}}((Y_{t},o_{t});H_{t-1}\mid z_{t-1},a_{t-1}); under (A1)–(A2), (Yt,ot)⟂(Ht−1,zt−1)|(Yt−1,at−1)(Y_{t},o_{t})\perp(H_{t-1},z_{t-1})\mid(Y_{t-1},a_{t-1}), so DPI on Ht−1→Yt−1→(Yt,ot)H_{t-1}\to Y_{t-1}\to(Y_{t},o_{t}) conditional on (zt−1,at−1)(z_{t-1},a_{t-1}) yields Iμθ((Yt,ot);Ht−1∣zt−1,at−1)≤Iμθ(Yt−1;Ht−1∣zt−1,at−1)≤Iμθ(Yt−1;Ht−1∣zt−1)I_{\mu_{\theta}}((Y_{t},o_{t});H_{t-1}\mid z_{t-1},a_{t-1})\leq I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t-1};H_{t-1}\mid z_{t-1},a_{t-1})\leq I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t-1};H_{t-1}\mid z_{t-1}) (using Theorem 1’s action-monotonicity step under (A3); the identical bound holds under post-turn dialogue indexing H~t=(zt−1,ot,at)\tilde{H}_{t}=(z_{t-1},o_{t},a_{t})). Finally, if KK admits an injective encoding e:ℬreach↪𝒵Ke:\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{reach}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{Z}_{K}, setting zk=e⁡(Φ⁡(e−1​(zk−1),ak−1,ok))z_{k}=e(\Phi(e^{-1}(z_{k-1}),a_{k-1},o_{k})) yields P⁡(Yk∣zk)=P⁡(Yk∣Hk)P(Y_{k}\mid z_{k})=P(Y_{k}\mid H_{k}) almost surely and supkIμθ​(Yk;Hk∣zk)=0\sup_{k}I_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{k};H_{k}\mid z_{k})=0. ∎

Corollary 1 (Suboptimality of Myopic Greedy Compression vs. Non-Myopic RL).

Consider a stream HT=(o1,…,oT)H_{T}=(o_{1},\dots,o_{T}) with mutually independent chunk targets YT=(Y(1),…,Y(T))Y_{T}=(Y^{(1)},\dots,Y^{(T)}) where Y(k)Y^{(k)} arrives in chunk ok=(Y(k),Nk)o_{k}=(Y^{(k)},N_{k}), 0<∑m=1TH⁡(Y(m))=H⁡(YT)≤K​log⁡|𝒱|0<\sum_{m=1}^{T}H(Y^{(m)})=H(Y_{T})\leq K\log|\mathcal{V}|, and nuisance details Nk⟂YTN_{k}\perp Y_{T} satisfy H⁡(Nk)>K​log⁡|𝒱|+log⁡2H(N_{k})>K\log|\mathcal{V}|+\log 2. A.5 Pointwise Mutual Information Identities and Critic Shift

Motivation and Intuition.

While Propositions 1 and 2 characterize MaxIM’s population objectives (−Hμθ​(Yt∣zt)-H_{\mu_{\theta}}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}) and Iμθ​(zt,H~t)I_{\mu_{\theta}}(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t})), our practical algorithm (Sections 4.3–4.4) optimizes step-wise pointwise mutual information (PMI) ratios scored by a frozen offline critic qϕq_{\phi} with masked null baselines (znull,H~nullz_{\mathrm{null}},\tilde{H}_{\mathrm{null}}), bounded sigmoid transformations, and mid-training cosine annealing. Proposition 6 bridges theory and implementation across three practical questions: (i) Why subtract log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣znull)\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{\mathrm{null}})? Raw log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣zt)\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{t}) conflates summary informativeness with inherent target difficulty; subtracting log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣znull)\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{\mathrm{null}}) acts as an exact per-step zero-mean baseline that cancels target difficulty without biasing the immediate policy gradient. (ii) What does forward consistency PMI optimize—and why does MI-Only RL still need RtaskR_{\text{task}}? Expanding the expected forward log-ratio recovers Iνθ​(zt,H~t)I_{\nu_{\theta}}(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t}) minus a conditional critic gap, plus +DKL(Pνθ(zt)∥qϕ(zt∣H~null))+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\nu_{\theta}}(z_{t})\,\|\,q_{\phi}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{\mathrm{null}})); this positive KL term explains why unanchored MI-Only RL (Rtask=0R_{\text{task}}=0, Section 5.4) can inflate consistency PMI by drifting toward telegraphic strings that are improbable under the masked prior qϕ(⋅∣H~null)q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid\tilde{H}_{\mathrm{null}}). (iii) How is offline critic shift controlled? KL regularization keeps νθ\nu_{\theta} close to ν𝒟\nu_{\mathcal{D}} early in RL while λs=1\lambda_{s}=1 resolves sparse credit assignment, and cosine annealing (λs→0\lambda_{s}\to 0) removes all residual critic and prior-mismatch bias in late training.

Proposition 6 (PMI Unbiasedness, Recursive Consistency, and Critic Shift).

Let qϕq_{\phi} be a frozen critic trained on offline distribution ν𝒟\nu_{\mathcal{D}} via Eq. (3), and let νθ\nu_{\theta} denote the marginal state-summary distribution under policy πθ\pi_{\theta}. Then:

  1. (i)

    Unbiased Immediate Sufficiency Baseline: Subtracting the length-normalized masked-summary baseline 1|Yt|​log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣znull)\frac{1}{|Y_{t}|}\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{\mathrm{null}}) in Eq. (4) satisfies 𝔼zt∼πθ(⋅∣H~t)[∇θlogπθ(zt∣H~t)1|Yt|logqϕ(Yt∣znull)]=0\mathbb{E}_{z_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\tilde{H}_{t})}\big[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t})\,\frac{1}{|Y_{t}|}\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{\mathrm{null}})\big]=0 conditional on (Ht,Yt)(H_{t},Y_{t}) (and across the full trajectory when targets are exogenous), preserving exact per-step policy-gradient unbiasedness for raw rpred,tr_{\text{pred},t} while canceling instance-level target entropy.

  2. (ii)

    Recursive Consistency Decomposition: Prior to 1/|zt|1/|z_{t}| length normalization (which rescales per-token values to avoid favoring verbose summaries), the expected sequence-level forward log-ratio satisfies

    𝔼νθ​[log⁡qϕ​(zt∣H~t)qϕ​(zt∣H~null)]=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{\theta}}\!\Big[\log\frac{q_{\phi}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t})}{q_{\phi}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{\mathrm{null}})}\Big]={} Iνθ(zt;H~t)−𝔼H~t[DKL(Pνθ(zt∣H~t)∥qϕ(zt∣H~t))]\displaystyle I_{\nu_{\theta}}(z_{t};\tilde{H}_{t})-\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{H}_{t}}\!\big[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\nu_{\theta}}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t})\,\|\,q_{\phi}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t}))\big] (23)
    +DKL(Pνθ(zt)∥qϕ(zt∣H~null)).\displaystyle+D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(P_{\nu_{\theta}}(z_{t})\,\|\,q_{\phi}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{\mathrm{null}})\big).
  3. (iii)

Part (i) and Practical Departures: Conditional on (Ht,Yt)(H_{t},Y_{t}), neither |Yt||Y_{t}| nor log⁡qϕ​(Yt∣znull)\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{\mathrm{null}}) depends on the sampled summary ztz_{t}, so 𝔼zt∼πθ(⋅∣H~t)[∇θlogπθ(zt∣H~t)1|Yt|logqϕ(Yt∣znull)]=1|Yt|logqϕ(Yt∣znull)∇θ∑ztπθ(zt∣H~t)=0\mathbb{E}_{z_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\tilde{H}_{t})}\big[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t})\,\frac{1}{|Y_{t}|}\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{\mathrm{null}})\big]=\frac{1}{|Y_{t}|}\log q_{\phi}(Y_{t}\mid z_{\mathrm{null}})\,\nabla_{\theta}\sum_{z_{t}}\pi_{\theta}(z_{t}\mid\tilde{H}_{t})=0, preserving unbiased immediate policy gradients while subtracting instance-level target difficulty to reduce gradient variance across prompts. In practice, Eq. (6) and Eq. (7) introduce two deliberate departures from a pure linear control variate: (1) in closed-loop dialogue, future baselines log⁡qϕ​(Yk∣znull)\log q_{\phi}(Y_{k}\mid z_{\mathrm{null}}) (k>tk>t) depend on ztz_{t} via ata_{t} and normalize future state difficulty so the policy is not rewarded for steering toward trivially low-entropy user states; and (2) passing rpred,tr_{\text{pred},t} and rcons,tr_{\text{cons},t} through centered sigmoids σ⁡(α⁡(r−b))−12\sigma(\alpha(r-b))-\tfrac{1}{2} makes the baseline nonlinear, trading exact variance-reduction linearity for bounded step-wise scale (preventing heavy-tailed log-ratio spikes) and zero-centered length neutrality on variable-horizon episodes.
