Part (iii): By the triangle inequality, data processing for TV (since νθ\nu_{\theta} is a marginal projection of μθ\mu_{\theta}), and Pinsker’s inequality, DTV​(νθ,ν𝒟)≤DTV​(νθ,νref)+DTV​(νref,ν𝒟)≤12DKL(μθ∥μref)+DTV​(νref,ν𝒟)D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\nu_{\theta},\nu_{\mathcal{D}})\leq D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\nu_{\theta},\nu_{\mathrm{ref}})+D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\nu_{\mathrm{ref}},\nu_{\mathcal{D}})\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu_{\theta}\,\|\,\mu_{\mathrm{ref}})}+D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\nu_{\mathrm{ref}},\nu_{\mathcal{D}}) (where training qϕq_{\phi} across high-quality, vague, and hallucinated summary tiers widens ν𝒟\nu_{\mathcal{D}} to reduce DTV​(νref,ν𝒟)D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\nu_{\mathrm{ref}},\nu_{\mathcal{D}})). Finally, under Eq. (24), λs=0\lambda_{s}=0 for all s≥sends\geq s_{\mathrm{end}}, identically removing all residual Δpost​(ϕ,θ)\Delta_{\mathrm{post}}(\phi;\theta) and masked-prior mismatch terms from Eq. (7) so late-stage PPO updates optimize the exact KL-regularized downstream task objective. ∎

Appendix B Synthetic Data Generation

A key advantage of MaxIM is that its dense reward signals are derived entirely from synthetic offline data, eliminating the need for expensive human preference labels. This appendix details the data generation pipelines for both benchmarks.

B.1 arXiv Data Generation

Paper Scraping, Chunk Segmentation, and Disjoint Splits.

We scrape recent papers from ar5iv [39], the HTML5 mirror of arXiv, in March 2026 and April–September 2026 across 9 diverse categories (cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.RO, eess.SY, math.OC, astro-ph.IM, q-bio.QM, physics.comp-ph) to ensure topical diversity and minimize parametric pretraining leakage. For each paper, we extract the main body prose (excluding the abstract, bibliography, and appendices) and segment it along paragraph and sentence boundaries into ≈500\approx 500-token chunks under the Gemini SentencePiece tokenizer, yielding up to 2525 chunks per paper. In total, we curate 2,1962{,}196 papers (≥20\geq 20 chunks): 1,8141{,}814 March 2026 papers partitioned strictly disjointly by salted MD5 hash (70%/30%70\%/30\%) into 1,2811{,}281 critic-training papers (used exclusively for offline critic pre-training and Policy SFT) and 533533 RL-training papers (used exclusively for online RL rollouts and Best-of-NN MI SFT with N=8N=8), 4444 validation papers for checkpoint selection, and 338338 post-cutoff held-out test papers (mean 24.5824.58 chunks/paper; 55 synthesis MCQs per paper). For the Early-Section Stress Test, we construct an analogous disjoint split (525525 RL train / 3636 validation / 332332 test papers) whose comprehension questions are derived strictly from body chunks 33–77 (excluding the Abstract and Introduction).

MCQ Generation and Anti-Leakage Calibration.

For each paper, we prompt an oracle model (Gemini 3.0 Flash) with the full paper text and request 5 synthesis-level multiple-choice questions requiring cross-section reasoning. Each question has 4 options (A–D) with exactly one correct answer. The prompt explicitly instructs the model to generate questions that cannot be answered from any single section alone, forcing the summarizer to retain cross-sectional information. To prevent frozen downstream solvers from exploiting option-length heuristics or parametric priors without reading the summary, we apply an automated distractor-rewrite pass enforcing ±10%\pm 10\% word/character parity across options A–D (with 11–22 distractors slightly longer than the gold answer), deterministically permute option order, and append a fifth abstention option E (“The summary does not contain enough information to answer this question”). This calibration reduces no-summary forced-choice accuracy from 67.5%67.5\% to 27.6%27.6\% (near the 25%25\% chance floor) and no-summary Abstain-MCQ accuracy to 2.6%2.6\% (91.9%91.9\% abstention). The full MCQ generation prompt is provided in Appendix E.

Three-Tier Summary Variants and Critic (Input,Target)(\text{Input},\text{Target}) Pairs.

At each turn tt of each critic-training paper, we synthesize three summary quality variants using an oracle model:

  1. 1.

    High-Quality (zthqz_{t}^{\text{hq}}): Generated with the paper prefix o1:to_{1:t} and MCQ context visible, instructing the oracle to retain the maximal task-relevant evidence within budget KK. These serve as positive targets for both sufficiency and recursive consistency, as well as Policy SFT supervision.

  2. 2.

    Vague (ztvaguez_{t}^{\text{vague}}): Generated by degrading zthqz_{t}^{\text{hq}} into a fluent but generic overview that omits specific technical mechanisms, equations, and quantitative results, calibrating the critic to penalize information-poor summaries.

  3. 3.

    Hallucinated (zthallucz_{t}^{\text{halluc}}): Generated by altering core claims and empirical findings in zthqz_{t}^{\text{hq}} into plausible but fabricated statements of matched style and length, calibrating the critic against confabulation.

To construct supervised (input,target)(\text{input},\text{target}) examples for Eq. (3) (training details in Appendix D.2; exact prompt templates in Appendix E.3), for every summary z∈{zthq,ztvague,zthalluc,znull}z\in\{z_{t}^{\text{hq}},z_{t}^{\text{vague}},z_{t}^{\text{halluc}},z_{\mathrm{null}}\} (where znull="(no summary available)"z_{\mathrm{null}}=\texttt{"(no summary available)"}), the frozen Abstain-MCQ action model answers the paper’s five questions Q1:5Q_{1:5} from zz alone, producing a distilled 5-letter answer sequence Y^​(z)∈{A,…,E}5\hat{Y}(z)\in\{\text{A},\dots,\text{E}\}^{5} (selecting E whenever zz lacks supporting evidence). Across the 1,2811{,}281 critic-training papers, 𝒟\mathcal{D} comprises 136,003136{,}003 examples across six subsets: (i) conditional sufficiency pairs ((zt,Q1:5),Y^(zt))\big((z_{t},Q_{1:5}),\,\hat{Y}(z_{t})\big) for zt∈{zthq,ztvague,zthalluc}z_{t}\in\{z_{t}^{\text{hq}},z_{t}^{\text{vague}},z_{t}^{\text{halluc}}\} (26,94926{,}949, 26,94926{,}949, and 26,92626{,}926 examples) plus masked-summary baselines ((znull,Q1:5),Y^(znull))\big((z_{\mathrm{null}},Q_{1:5}),\,\hat{Y}(z_{\mathrm{null}})\big) (1,2811{,}281 examples, one per paper); and (ii) forward recursive consistency pairs ((zt−1hq,ot),zthq)\big((z_{t-1}^{\text{hq}},o_{t}),\,z_{t}^{\text{hq}}\big) (26,94926{,}949 examples, with z0hq=∅z_{0}^{\text{hq}}=\varnothing) plus masked-context baselines (H~null,zthq)\big(\tilde{H}_{\mathrm{null}},\,z_{t}^{\text{hq}}\big) (26,94926{,}949 examples, replacing both context fields with "(not available)").

B.2 WildChat Data Generation

Seed Data, Disjoint Partitioning, and Trajectory Regeneration.

We use WildChat [40] conversations as seeds. Specifically, we extract English conversations with ≥6\geq 6 user turns (7,9687{,}968 validated dialogues) and prompt an annotator model (Gemini 3.0 Flash) sequentially at each turn tt with the observable dialogue prefix up to turn tt and prior state st−1s_{t-1} to causally annotate the user’s evolving internal state. To test out-of-distribution generalization to unseen user personas, 500500 full dialogues are held out from user-simulator training, from which 200200 form our unseen-simulator OOD evaluation split. The remaining 7,4687{,}468 simulator-training dialogues train the user simulator and are partitioned strictly disjointly into 3,0003{,}000 critic/SFT seed dialogues (2,9282{,}928 rolled out into 25,49725{,}497 turns for critic and Policy SFT training, plus 2,5112{,}511 held-out critic validation triplets), 3,5003{,}500 RL seed dialogues for online RL, 200200 validation dialogues, 500500 held-out test dialogues, and 268268 offline PMI-calibration seeds. Because the original WildChat conversations were generated with an assistant model to which we do not have access, we synthetically regenerate full multi-turn trajectories using an action agent and a trained user simulator (Appendix D.1). This creates a controlled closed-loop environment where we have access to ground-truth user internal states at every turn.

Dynamic Conversation Generation.

Each conversation proceeds for up to 1212 turns during RL training and up to 1515 turns at evaluation (testing +25%+25\% horizon extrapolation), initialized with z0=∅z_{0}=\varnothing and persona s0s_{0}, via the following loop for turn t=1,2,…t=1,2,\dots:

  1. 1.

    The user simulator generates the next user utterance utu_{t} conditioned on prior latent state st−1s_{t-1} and conversation history. If the simulator outputs a termination signal, the episode ends.

  2. 2.

    The action agent generates a response ata_{t} conditioned on the conversation context and the summarizer’s prior belief estimate zt−1z_{t-1} injected into its system prompt (no belief injected at t=1t=1, since z0=∅z_{0}=\varnothing).

  3. 3.

    Given user observation ot=uto_{t}=u_{t} and assistant action ata_{t}, the summarizer policy updates the post-turn belief zt∼πθ(⋅∣zt−1,ot,at)z_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid z_{t-1},o_{t},a_{t}) (post-action turn indexing so ztz_{t} aligns with post-turn user state sts_{t}), and the user simulator updates sts_{t} (YtY_{t}).

Belief Summary Variants and 10-Key Schema.

Analogous to the arXiv pipeline, we generate three quality tiers of belief summaries (HQ, vague, hallucinated) plus masked-context baseline queries (znull,H~nullz_{\mathrm{null}},\tilde{H}_{\mathrm{null}}) at each turn using an oracle model with access to the true user internal states. Belief states are structured as canonical 10-key probabilistic JSON objects inside <state>...</state> tags: core_intent_functional_goal, affective_state_perceived_stakes, user_expertise_epistemic_stance, cognitive_demand_information_specificity, interaction_strategy_communication_demeanor, agent_perception_trust_output_control, task_state_domain_context, patience_reserve_accumulator, task_success_outlook, and specific_needs_and_constraints. For vague sufficiency examples, four keys are degraded to generic placeholders paired with <insufficient_information> targets; for hallucinated sufficiency examples, four keys receive orthogonal distractor traits, enforcing strict critic conditioning on ztz_{t}.

Appendix C MaxIM Training Algorithm

Algorithm 1 details the complete three-phase pipeline for training the MaxIM agent, including offline synthetic data generation, unified critic pre-training, and KL-regularized PPO policy optimization with mid-training cosine annealing.

Appendix D Details of Experiments

D.1 User Simulator

The WildChat user simulator is trained via SFT on the offline WildChat dataset [40], where per-turn internal state annotations were first generated by an oracle annotator model. Specifically, we train a unified joint state-and-response user simulator (initialized from Gemini 2.5 Flash and fine-tuned for 66 epochs on the 7,4687{,}468 simulator-training dialogues). At each turn, conditioned on the initial persona s0s_{0} and full dialogue history, the simulator emits a structured trace <think><impact>...</impact><dimensions>{10-key JSON}</dimensions></think> followed immediately by the next natural-language user utterance (or a termination token) in a single call. Up to two schema-validation resamples ensure 100%100\% canonical 10-key ground-truth state coverage across multi-turn rollouts (median length 8.08.0 turns).

D.2 Critic Training

The variational critic qϕq_{\phi} is trained via standard cross-entropy minimization over target tokens only (masking prompt and instruction tokens). Rather than maintaining separate checkpoints for sufficiency and consistency, each benchmark trains a single unified Gemini 2.5 Flash critic on a six-way multi-task mixture (assigning unit sampling weight 1.01.0 to HQ, vague, and hallucinated conditional sufficiency examples as well as conditional and masked-context grounding examples, and weight 0.050.05 to masked-summary sufficiency baselines):

  • •

    Sufficiency PMI (rpred,tr_{\text{pred},t}): On arXiv, qϕq_{\phi} scores the mean log-likelihood of the 55 single-token Abstain-MCQ target letters (A–E) conditioned on ztz_{t} minus the cached masked-summary baseline (zt=znullz_{t}=z_{\mathrm{null}}). On WildChat, qϕq_{\phi} scores the per-token log-likelihood of the canonical 10-key post-turn true user state sts_{t} conditioned on ztz_{t} minus the masked-state baseline (znullz_{\mathrm{null}}).

  • •

    Recursive Consistency PMI (rcons,tr_{\text{cons},t}): On both benchmarks, qϕq_{\phi} scores the per-token log-likelihood of the generated summary ztz_{t} conditioned on local context H~t\tilde{H}_{t} (H~t=(zt−1,ot)\tilde{H}_{t}=(z_{t-1},o_{t}) on arXiv; H~t=(zt−1,ot,at)\tilde{H}_{t}=(z_{t-1},o_{t},a_{t}) on WildChat) minus its masked-context baseline conditioned on H~null\tilde{H}_{\mathrm{null}}.

Training uses three quality tiers—HQ, vague, and hallucinated—so the critic sees the full spectrum of summary quality during training. We use single-epoch offline training (≤1\leq 1 epoch over HQ targets) to prevent memorization. The same critic checkpoint is shared across all shaped RL conditions within a benchmark. While we train one unified critic per benchmark here for clean experimental isolation, because Eq. (3) routes tasks purely through natural-language system instructions over token cross-entropy, the same architecture directly supports joint multi-task and cross-domain critic training.

D.3 RL Hyperparameters and Implementation Details

Reward Transformation, Offline Calibration, and Annealing.

To combine sufficiency and consistency PMI scores on a common bounded scale while centering neutral summaries at zero, we evaluate initial pre-RL base-policy rollouts strictly offline to compute the mean midpoint bb and within-prompt standard deviation σwithin\sigma_{\text{within}} for each PMI signal, setting slope α=1/σwithin\alpha=1/\sigma_{\text{within}} and mapping each signal to σ⁡(α⁡(r−b))−12∈[−0.5,+0.5]\sigma(\alpha(r-b))-\tfrac{1}{2}\in[-0.5,+0.5] (eliminating positive survival-length bias on variable-horizon WildChat dialogues). On arXiv (K=500K=500), this yields (bs,bc)=(−0.28,1.71)(b_{s},b_{c})=(-0.28,1.71) and (αs,αc)=(2.85,7.95)(\alpha_{s},\alpha_{c})=(2.85,7.95) (with budget-specific midpoints bs∈{−0.79,−0.43,−0.28,−0.10}b_{s}\in\{-0.79,-0.43,-0.28,-0.10\} and bc∈{2.02,1.78,1.71,1.68}b_{c}\in\{2.02,1.78,1.71,1.68\} for K∈{100,300,500,800}K\in\{100,300,500,800\}, and bs=−0.72b_{s}=-0.72 on the Early-Section Stress Test); on WildChat, (bs,bc)=(0.0921,0.4950)(b_{s},b_{c})=(0.0921,0.4950) and (αs,αc)=(33.53,4.36)(\alpha_{s},\alpha_{c})=(33.53,4.36). Across both domains, we use MI weights (ws,wc)=(0.30,0.11)(w_{s},w_{c})=(0.30,0.11) alongside Rtask∈[0,1]R_{\text{task}}\in[0,1], discount γ=0.9\gamma=0.9, step-shaping scale ηshape=1−γ=0.1\eta_{\text{shape}}=1-\gamma=0.1 to account for multi-turn reward accumulation, and cosine annealing λs\lambda_{s} holding 1.01.0 through step sstart=450s_{\text{start}}=450 before decaying smoothly to 0.00.0 at step send=600s_{\text{end}}=600:

λs={1,s≤sstart,12​(1+cos⁡(π​s−sstartsend−sstart)),sstart<s<send,0,s≥send.\lambda_{s}=\begin{cases}1,&s\leq s_{\text{start}},\\ \frac{1}{2}\!\left(1+\cos\!\left(\pi\frac{s-s_{\text{start}}}{s_{\text{end}}-s_{\text{start}}}\right)\right),&s_{\text{start}}<s<s_{\text{end}},\\ 0,&s\geq s_{\text{end}}.\end{cases} (24)

In addition, to enforce valid XML delimiters during RL across all methods, a lightweight tag-formatting penalty (weight 0.050.05, scaled by 0.10.1) assigns 00 when complete <summary>...</summary> (arXiv) or <state>...</state> (WildChat) tags are present, −0.5-0.5 if only one tag is present, and −1.0-1.0 if neither is present.

Advantage Normalization.

Table 4 summarizes our training and evaluation settings. For group-relative advantage estimation across G=8G=8 rollouts per prompt, let 𝒢t={j∈{1,…,G}:Tj≥t}\mathcal{G}_{t}=\{j\in\{1,\dots,G\}:T_{j}\geq t\} denote active trajectories at turn tt. Whenever |𝒢t|≥2|\mathcal{G}_{t}|\geq 2, we compute an exact leave-one-out baseline A~i,t=Gt(i)−1|𝒢t|−1​∑j∈𝒢t∖{i}Gt(j)\tilde{A}_{i,t}=G_{t}^{(i)}-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}_{t}|-1}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{G}_{t}\setminus\{i\}}G_{t}^{(j)} (setting A~i,t=0\tilde{A}_{i,t}=0 if |𝒢t|<2|\mathcal{G}_{t}|<2) and normalize by the prompt-wide standard deviation across all valid turn-rollout pairs in the group, avoiding noisy small-sample variance division at late turns. Policies are updated using KL-regularized PPO [37].

Optimization and Computational Overhead.

Computing the step-wise variational rewards requires only teacher-forced forward passes through the critic transformer, avoiding expensive autoregressive generation. To ensure we do not block environment trajectory generation, critic reward computation is executed asynchronously across distributed inference servers and collected at episode end.

D.4 Evaluation Protocol, Training Compute, and Inference Cost

Task Metrics, Bounded-Memory Multi-Turn Dialogue, and Causal Belief Scoring.

For arXiv, a frozen action model answers 5 MCQs conditioned only on the final summary. Under our primary Abstain-MCQ protocol (options A–E), correct answers earn +1+1, abstentions (E) earn 00, and wrong commitments (A–D) incur −1/3-1/3. For WildChat, because evaluating a conversational agent spans multiple distinct quality axes (goal fulfillment, constraint adherence, coherence) and collapsing them into a single scalar reward risks misspecification, during RL training an oracle rater (Gemini 3.0 Flash) receives (s0,u1,a1,s1,z1,…,sT,zT)(s_{0},u_{1},a_{1},s_{1},z_{1},\dots,s_{T},z_{T}) under a strict causal 1​…​t1\dots t grounding rule (never penalizing ztz_{t} for traits revealed at turns >t>t) and outputs 11–1010 belief accuracy ratings (rescaled to [0,1][0,1] as RtaskR_{\text{task}}, and reported in Table 10). At test time (RQ1, Tables 1 and 9), to evaluate downstream conversational utility under bounded context without retraining the assistant, we execute fresh rollouts (T≤15T\leq 15) on the N=500N=500 held-out test split where the frozen Gemini 2.5 Flash assistant receives only the single preceding user–assistant interaction (k=1k=1: (ut−1,at−1)(u_{t-1},a_{t-1})) and the latest user message utu_{t} together with zt−1z_{t-1} (whereas the No-Belief baseline receives only (ut−1,at−1,ut)(u_{t-1},a_{t-1},u_{t})). An independent GPT-4.1 evaluator (temperature=0\text{temperature}=0), conditioned strictly on (u1:T,a1:T)(u_{1:T},a_{1:T}) and ground-truth user states s0:Ts_{0:T} without access to ztz_{t} or method identity, rates each session (11–1010) on Goal Completion, Preference & Constraint Retention, Coherence & Adaptability, and Overall User Satisfaction. Statistical significance between paired conversation seeds is computed via 10,00010{,}000-resample paired bootstrap on both all N=500N=500 seeds and the fixed T≥10T\geq 10 cohort (N=158N=158 seeds where No-Belief requires T≥10T\geq 10 turns).

Qualitative Autorater and Atomic-Claim Grounding Protocols.

For qualitative evaluation (Table 2, Appendix F.4), a cross-family GPT-4.1 judge (temperature=0\text{temperature}=0) compares candidate summaries conditioned on identical observed prefixes up to turn tt with randomized A/B order on Truthfulness and Usefulness, and independently scores each policy’s single-step transition (zt−1,ot)→zt(z_{t-1},o_{t})\to z_{t} on a 11–1010 Consistency scale so ratings are not confounded by differences in zt−1z_{t-1} (prompts in Appendix E). While our evaluation pipeline computes all three qualitative metrics on both tasks, Table 2 reports Consistency on arXiv and Truthfulness on WildChat due to complementary ceiling effects: on arXiv prose summaries, factual precision saturates near ceiling across RL methods (97.5%97.5\%–98.4%98.4\% entailment) whereas Consistency strongly separates policies (5.995.99–7.557.55); conversely, on WildChat’s fixed 10-key JSON schema, standalone Consistency saturates near ceiling across all RL policies (9.699.69–9.869.86; Appendix F.4) whereas Truthfulness varies substantially (36.2%36.2\%–72.4%72.4\%). For atomic-claim grounding, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite (temperature=0\text{temperature}=0) first decomposes each candidate summary ztz_{t}—and, for chunk claim incorporation (Figure 2(b), Table 7), each incoming source chunk oto_{t} (extracted once per paper and shared across all methods)—into standalone, de-contextualized atomic factual claims; GPT-4.1 then classifies each claim against the observed source prefix as ENTAILED, NEUTRAL, or CONTRADICTED via natural language inference (NLI), complemented by a Gemini 3.0 Flash cross-check on arXiv (Appendix F.4).

Training and Inference Computational Complexity.

All SFT, RL, and serving jobs run on Google Cloud TPU accelerators. Let SmaxS_{\max} denote the total number of online RL update steps (Smax=1,000S_{\max}=1{,}000 on arXiv and Smax=800S_{\max}=800 on WildChat) and NparamN_{\text{param}} denote the active parameter count of the shared Gemini 2.5 Flash backbone used across every trainable policy, unified critic, action agent, and user simulator. Because shared-cluster wall-clock duration fluctuates with serving-replica concurrency, Table 5 reports hardware-independent relative training FLOPs normalized to sparse-reward RL (1.00×1.00\times) under standard transformer accounting (2​Nparam2N_{\text{param}} FLOPs per forward/decode token, 6​Nparam6N_{\text{param}} per forward-backward training token, plus 2​Nparam2N_{\text{param}} PPO reference evaluation). Because critic passes are teacher-forced log-likelihood evaluations (2​Nparam2N_{\text{param}}/token, zero decoding), masked baselines are cached once per episode, and cosine annealing sets λs=0\lambda_{s}=0 for s≥600s\geq 600, MaxIM requires only ≈1.25×\approx 1.25\times total training FLOPs on arXiv (1.23×1.23\times online RL plus 0.02×0.02\times one-time critic SFT) and ≈1.17×\approx 1.17\times on WildChat (1.14×1.14\times online RL plus 0.03×0.03\times critic SFT) relative to Task-Only/MemAgent RL, adding <15%<15\% per-step RL wall-clock overhead during s<600s<600 (0%0\% for s≥600s\geq 600). Beyond the final benchmark runs in Table 5, preliminary development (data-pipeline validation, reward-weight and annealing sweeps) consumed roughly 2.5×2.5\times the compute of the reported experiments. At deployment, test-time inference incurs zero critic overhead (1.00×1.00\times FLOPs and latency): every method executes the same single summarizer call per turn (O⁡(T⋅K)O(T\cdot K) generated tokens), avoiding the O⁡(T2​Lchunk)O(T^{2}L_{\text{chunk}}) quadratic attention cost of full-context prompting.

Appendix E Prompt Templates

This appendix documents the prompt templates used across MaxIM’s summarizer policies, synthetic data pipelines, variational critics, and evaluation judges. Template variables injected at runtime are denoted in monospace braces (e.g., {max_summary_tokens}).

E.1 Incremental Summarizer Policy Prompts

At each turn tt, the summarizer policy πθ\pi_{\theta} receives a domain-specific system prompt and a user message containing the previous summary zt−1z_{t-1} alongside the latest chunk or dialogue exchange. On WildChat, the output inside <state>...</state> follows the 10-key JSON schema defined in Appendix B.2.

E.2 Offline Benchmark Synthesis Prompt

To construct cross-section comprehension targets for arXiv (Appendix B.1), Gemini 3.0 Flash generates five synthesis-level MCQs from the full paper text prior to distractor length-parity calibration and option-E augmentation.

E.3 Unified Critic Prompts for PMI Estimation

As described in Section 4.3 and Appendix D.2, a single unified critic checkpoint qϕq_{\phi} per benchmark handles all four conditional and null-baseline log-likelihood queries in Eqs. (4)–(5). Cross-entropy training loss and RL teacher-forced scoring are applied strictly to the Target tokens; null baselines replace the conditioning summary or local context with fixed placeholder strings ("(no summary available)", "(no state estimate available)", or "(not available)").

E.4 Downstream Task Evaluation Prompts

At test time, arXiv terminal summaries zTz_{T} are evaluated by the frozen Abstain-MCQ action model, and WildChat bounded-memory (k=1k=1) conversations are scored by an independent GPT-4.1 judge that never observes ztz_{t}.

E.5 Atomic-Claim Grounding and Qualitative Autorater Prompts

Our source-grounding pipeline (Section 5.3, Appendix D.4) first decomposes passages into standalone atomic claims using Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite and then verifies source entailment in batched NLI calls using GPT-4.1 (or Gemini 3.0 Flash). Qualitative evaluation uses GPT-4.1 for randomized A/B pairwise judging (Truthfulness, Usefulness) and standalone 11–1010 Consistency scoring.

F.1 Full Token-Budget Scaling and Chunk Claim Incorporation

At K=500K=500 (66.39%66.39\%, 427.7427.7 tokens), MaxIM surpasses Prompt-Only even at K=2,000K=2{,}000 (64.32%64.32\%, 1,453.31{,}453.3 tokens; 3.4×\mathbf{3.4\times} compression gain) before saturating at 67.04%67.04\% (K=800K=800), consistent with Proposition 4. F.4 Turn-Stratified Qualitative and Cross-Judge Grounding Evaluation

Cross-Family Grounding Verification.

To verify that Table 2’s arXiv grounding results are not specific to GPT-4.1, we re-evaluate terminal-zTz_{T} atomic-claim entailment using Gemini 3.0 Flash. We observe the exact same pattern: all RL policies maintain high factual precision—98.43%98.43\% (Suff-Only RL), 98.19%98.19\% (MemAgent RL), 98.14%98.14\% (Task-Only RL), 97.77%97.77\% (MI-Only RL), and 96.76%96.76\% (MaxIM), alongside 98.44%98.44\% for Prompt-Only—whereas Policy SFT drops to 74.70%74.70\% as imitation errors compound over 2525 updates.

Turn-Stratified Qualitative Dynamics.

Table 11 tracks GPT-4.1 qualitative ratings across intermediate and terminal turns on both benchmarks. On arXiv (Table 11(a)), Policy SFT achieves high Usefulness at t=3t=3 (77.0%77.0\%) while summaries remain short, but collapses to 13.4%13.4\% by t=20t=20 as ungrounded claims accumulate. By contrast, MaxIM climbs from 39.0%39.0\% (t=3t=3) to 78.0%78.0\% (t=15t=15) and 72.9%72.9\% (t=20t=20) against Prompt-Only while achieving the highest standalone Consistency score (7.557.55 vs. 5.995.99–6.446.44 across other RL methods). Furthermore, when GPT-4.1 compares MaxIM directly against MemAgent on the exact same paper prefixes, MaxIM wins on Usefulness at every evaluated chunk (72.0%72.0\% at t=3t=3 through 54.8%54.8\% at t=20t=20, plus a 61.6%61.6\% Consistency win rate at t=20t=20).

On WildChat (Table 11(b)), standalone 11–1010 Consistency saturates near ceiling across all RL policies (9.699.69–9.869.86 vs. 9.649.64 for Prompt-Only and 9.379.37 for Policy SFT; MaxIM scores 9.73±0.049.73\pm 0.04) because unchanged fields of the 10-key JSON state carry forward smoothly across turns. Pairwise Usefulness and Truthfulness reveal a clear horizon crossover: at early turns (t=3,5t=3,5), Task-Only RL’s speculative trait guesses slightly edge MaxIM on Usefulness (82.1%82.1\% vs. 79.5%79.5\% at t=5t=5) at the cost of lower Truthfulness (70.5%70.5\% vs. 78.6%\mathbf{78.6\%}). Once conversations extend to t≥8t\geq 8, MaxIM leads every baseline on both Usefulness (76.4%76.4\%–90.2%90.2\%) and Truthfulness (71.5%71.5\%–88.5%88.5\%).

Appendix G Broader Impacts and Limitations

G.1 Broader Impacts

MaxIM introduces a principled approach to bounded memory management in streaming environments. On the positive side, this framework enhances the reliability of long-horizon AI agents by actively suppressing hallucinations and enforcing factual grounding through recursive consistency. This is particularly beneficial for high-stakes applications requiring persistent context—such as educational tutoring, accessibility tools, and medical or legal document analysis—where unbounded context scaling is computationally prohibitive.

However, the capability to persistently track dynamically evolving latent states (such as user emotions or implicit intents, as demonstrated in our WildChat experiments) poses potential privacy and surveillance risks. If deployed without safeguards, agents equipped with highly effective intent-tracking memory could be used for manipulative profiling or invasive monitoring. Furthermore, because the memory update relies heavily on its own prior state, early biases or misinterpretations encoded in the summary may compound over time. Mitigating these risks requires transparent user consent for long-term memory tracking, routine auditing of the internal summary states for bias or sensitive personal information, and the implementation of robust safety filters on the downstream action agent.

G.2 Limitations

While MaxIM effectively mitigates credit assignment failures through information-theoretic shaping, we acknowledge several limitations that provide avenues for future work:

  • •

    The Markovian approximation and irreversible loss: MaxIM enforces a strict Markovian bottleneck by conditioning solely on the immediate local context H~t=(zt−1,at−1,ot)\tilde{H}_{t}=(z_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t}). During inference, if the policy erroneously discards a critical piece of information at step tt, the loss is irreversible because the model lacks attention mechanisms to re-access Ht−2H_{t-2}. Pairing MaxIM’s compressed working memory with an external episodic retrieval fallback is a promising hybrid architecture for deployment.

  • •

    Oracle dependency for critic training: MaxIM circumvents the need for expensive human preference labels, shifting supervision to an offline synthetic pipeline (Appendix B) where privileged target variables YtY_{t} are available strictly during training. Applying MaxIM to a new domain requires defining a task-relevant target proxy YtY_{t} and generating offline critic data; as quantified in Proposition 3 of Appendix A.1, misspecifying YtY_{t} introduces an additive mediation floor proportional to (εr,εT)(\varepsilon_{r},\varepsilon_{T}).

  • •

    Training compute overhead: While step-wise teacher-forced PMI rewards eliminate autoregressive critic generation and incur zero test-time overhead (Table 5), the RL fine-tuning phase requires critic forward passes during the shaping window (s<600s<600), adding training compute relative to sparse-reward RL.

  • •

    LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation bias: Using a single model family for both policy training and qualitative evaluation can introduce self-preference bias. To mitigate this risk, we conduct atomic-claim source grounding and qualitative evaluations using an independent cross-family judge (GPT-4.1) alongside Gemini 3.0 Flash; nonetheless, live human-in-the-loop user studies would further complement simulated multi-turn benchmarks.
